The Avió, circling on its arm since 1928 — modelled, the story goes, on the first plane to fly Barcelona–Madrid. Nobody has ever landed it.
The Carrusel: painted horses, gilt mirrors and a wheezing organ. A small boy waves every single time he passes.

The Font de Canaletes: a cast-iron fountain with four taps. Legend says whoever drinks from it will always return to Barcelona. Sandra takes a sip, just in case.
Glòria's flower stall: buckets of roses, sunflowers and eucalyptus, and a hand-lettered sign: FLORS · FLOWERS · FLEURS.

Joan Miró's mosaic, set into the Rambla pavement at the Pla de l'Os in 1976: bold circles of red, blue and yellow that thousands of people walk over every day without noticing.
A café table on the terrassa, with a sugar bowl and a small ashtray full of olive stones.

PARC D'ATRACCIONS DEL TIBIDABO. Opened in 1901 on the highest summit of Collserola, 512 metres up. The name comes from the Latin 'tibi dabo' — 'I will give you'. The Avió, a replica aeroplane from 1928, still circles over the city. Beside the park rises the Temple del Sagrat Cor, finished in 1961.

LA CASCADA — PARC DE LA CIUTADELLA. Built between 1875 and 1888 by Josep Fontserè; a young architecture student called Antoni Gaudí worked on it. The gilded Quadriga de l'Aurora crowns it. The park stands where Philip V's citadel rose after 1714, and it hosted the 1888 Universal Exhibition.

BUILDINGS.name: Sagrada Família
BUILDINGS.plaque: BASÍLICA DE LA SAGRADA FAMÍLIA. Begun in 1882; Antoni Gaudí took charge in 1883 and gave the rest of his life to it. He is buried in its crypt. As an 'expiatory temple' it is paid for entirely by donations and visitors' tickets. Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it as a basilica in 2010.

BUILDINGS.name: MNAC
BUILDINGS.plaque: MUSEU NACIONAL D'ART DE CATALUNYA. Housed in the Palau Nacional, built for the 1929 International Exhibition. It holds one of the world's great collections of Romanesque wall painting, lifted from Pyrenean churches in the 1920s — among them the apse of Sant Climent de Taüll.

BUILDINGS.name: Universitat Pompeu Fabra
BUILDINGS.plaque: UNIVERSITAT POMPEU FABRA — Ciutadella campus. Founded in 1990 and named after Pompeu Fabra (1868–1948), who codified modern Catalan. The campus reuses old military barracks, and its library fills the Dipòsit de les Aigües, an 1880s reservoir by Josep Fontserè. Department of Economics and Business.

BUILDINGS.name: Parc de la Ciutadella
BUILDINGS.plaque: LA CASCADA — PARC DE LA CIUTADELLA. Built between 1875 and 1888 by Josep Fontserè; a young architecture student called Antoni Gaudí worked on it. The gilded Quadriga de l'Aurora crowns it. The park stands where Philip V's citadel rose after 1714, and it hosted the 1888 Universal Exhibition.

BUILDINGS.name: Casa Vicens
BUILDINGS.plaque: CASA VICENS. Gaudí's first major house, built 1883–1885 as a summer home for the stockbroker Manuel Vicens. Moorish in spirit, it is clad in green-and-white tiles and ceramic yellow marigolds. It opened to the public as a museum in 2017.

BUILDINGS.name: Casa Calvet
BUILDINGS.plaque: CASA CALVET. Built by Gaudí in 1898–1900 for the family of the textile manufacturer Pere Màrtir Calvet. His most conventional building — and the one that won Barcelona's first Annual Buildings Prize, in 1900. The carved mushrooms over the door honour the family's love of mycology.

BUILDINGS.name: Palau Güell
BUILDINGS.plaque: PALAU GÜELL. Built 1886–1888 by the young Gaudí for the industrialist Eusebi Güell, his great patron. Two parabolic arches let the carriages in; up on the roof, twenty chimneys wear bright trencadís mosaic. UNESCO World Heritage since 1984.

BUILDINGS.name: Casa Milà
BUILDINGS.plaque: CASA MILÀ — LA PEDRERA. Built by Gaudí for Pere Milà and Roser Segimon, 1906–1912. Its rippling stone front earned the nickname 'the stone quarry'. On the roof, sculpted chimneys stand guard like helmeted warriors. UNESCO World Heritage since 1984.

BUILDINGS.name: Casa Batlló
BUILDINGS.plaque: CASA BATLLÓ. Remodelled by Gaudí for the textile magnate Josep Batlló, 1904–1906. Locals call it the Casa dels Ossos, the House of Bones, for its skeletal balconies. The scaly roof is often read as the dragon slain by Sant Jordi — the turret with its cross is his lance.

BUILDINGS.name: Cafè Berlín
BUILDINGS.plaque: CAFÈ BERLÍN — Bakery & coffee. 'Pa de tota la vida, i també del de fora.' (Bread of a lifetime, and some from abroad.)

BUILDINGS.name: Llibreria El Drac
BUILDINGS.plaque: LLIBRERIA EL DRAC — new and second-hand books since 1961. A small brass dragon curls around the door handle.

BUILDINGS.name: Torrons Casa Joan
BUILDINGS.plaque: TORRONS CASA JOAN — artisan nougat, almonds toasted daily. 'El torró de tota la vida.'

BUILDINGS.name: Cafè de la Rambla
BUILDINGS.plaque: CAFÈ DE LA RAMBLA — coffee, pastries and, the chalkboard insists, the finest crema catalana in Barcelona.

BUILDINGS.name: Carrefour Express
BUILDINGS.plaque: CARREFOUR EXPRESS — Gran Via. Open every day. A sticker on the glass: 'Pfand / Deposit refund desk inside — €1 per bottle.'

BUILDINGS.name: Torrons del Mar
BUILDINGS.plaque: TORRONS DEL MAR — soft nougat by the sea. A hand-painted anchor sits beneath the name.

BUILDINGS.name: Sandra & Rosa
BUILDINGS.plaque: FLOR DEL ILIRI, 4. The doorbell reads SANDRA & ROSA. Under it, a little paper German flag has been taped on, very slightly crooked. Home.

BUILDINGS.name: Alba's flat
BUILDINGS.plaque: CARRER DE VALÈNCIA, 2 — across from the Ciutadella. One buzzer has a pressed flower sellotaped beside it: ALBA.

BUILDINGS.name: Maria's flat
BUILDINGS.plaque: CARRER D'ARAGÓ, 58. The buzzer label is typed, laminated and perfectly level: MARIA. Of course it is.

BUILDINGS.name: Alice's flat
BUILDINGS.plaque: CARRER DE BALMES, 128. A note under the buzzer: 'ALICE — ring twice, I'm probably asleep.'

BUILDINGS.name: Alessandra's flat
BUILDINGS.plaque: PASSEIG DE GRÀCIA, 47. The buzzer says ALESSANDRA in looping handwriting, with a small star drawn after it.

coffee.name: Cafè sol
coffee.desc: A short, dark espresso in a thick white cup. Barcelona drinks it standing at the bar, in three sips, with purpose.

croissant.name: Croissant
croissant.desc: Buttery, flaky, faintly warm. It leaves a small golden landslide on everything it touches.

oj.name: Orange juice
oj.desc: Freshly squeezed Valencian oranges. Bright enough to count as a sunrise.

crema.name: Crema catalana
crema.desc: A chilled citrus-and-cinnamon custard under a torched, glassy caramel crust. It cost €15 and it knows it.

vollkorn.name: Vollkornbrot
vollkorn.desc: Dense German wholegrain rye, heavy as a good argument. A slice of home, eleven hundred miles south.

torro_joan.name: Torró de Casa Joan
torro_joan.desc: Hard almond torró from Casa Joan: whole toasted almonds set in honey and egg white. Snaps like a promise.

torro_mar.name: Torró del Mar
torro_mar.desc: Soft Xixona-style torró from Torrons del Mar, ground almonds and honey, smooth as sand at low tide.

neules.name: Neules
neules.desc: Crisp rolled wafers, the kind Catalans dip in cava at Christmas. Shatter-prone. Worth it.

carquinyolis.name: Carquinyolis
carquinyolis.desc: Twice-baked almond biscuits, hard enough to be dunked without fear. A seaside snack for patient teeth.

apple.name: Apple
apple.desc: A crisp red apple from Lleida, where half of Catalonia's fruit seems to grow.

orange.name: Orange
orange.desc: A heavy, sweet Valencian orange. Peels in one long satisfying spiral if you're careful.

banana.name: Banana
banana.desc: A small speckled banana from the Canary Islands, sweeter than the big ones and proud of it.

bread.name: Barra de pa
bread.desc: A crusty white loaf, still warm. Rub it with tomato, olive oil and salt and you have pa amb tomàquet.

milk.name: Milk
milk.desc: A small carton of fresh milk. Cold, calm, uncomplicated.

choc.name: Chocolate bar
choc.desc: Dark chocolate with toasted almonds. Barcelona has been serious about chocolate since the 1700s.

cheese.name: Formatge
cheese.desc: A wedge of Catalan cheese from the Pyrenees, nutty and firm. Pairs well with bread and ambition.

water.name: Water
water.desc: A bottle of cold mineral water from Montseny. Not glamorous. Absolutely necessary.

cafe_llet.name: Cafè amb llet
cafe_llet.desc: Coffee with plenty of hot milk, from the museum café. The drink of a slow, contented morning.

chupa.name: Chupa Chups
chupa.desc: A strawberry lollipop. The brand was born near Barcelona in 1958; Salvador Dalí designed its daisy logo.

rye.name: Rye flour
rye.desc: A 5 kg sack of rye flour. Heavy, dusty, and exactly what a German baker's dreams are made of.

bottle.name: Empty bottle
bottle.desc: An empty deposit bottle. Worth €1 at the Pfand desk in Carrefour Express on the Gran Via.

shell.name: Seashell
shell.desc: A ridged scallop shell, sun-bleached pink and cream. Salva the beachcomber pays €1 apiece.

flower.name: Wildflower
flower.desc: A bright orange wildflower from the grass. Roser the botanist buys them; others might value them too.

bike_chain.name: Bicycle chain
bike_chain.desc: A new bicycle chain in an oily paper wrap, collected from Genís for Jordi the bike mechanic.

brush.name: Sable brush
brush.desc: A tiny, very expensive sable-hair brush with a restorer's initials — C.F. — scratched into the handle.

balloon.name: Laia's balloon
balloon.desc: A red balloon on a curly ribbon, rescued from the Ferris wheel. It bobs cheerfully at your shoulder.

textbook.name: Principles of Economics
textbook.desc: Prof. Oriol's textbook, heavily annotated in green ink. Alice has pressed a get-well card inside as a bookmark.

cap.name: Tomàs's cap
cap.desc: A salt-stained fisherman's cap, navy blue, with a brass anchor on the band. It smells faintly of the sea.

camera_marta.name: Marta's camera
camera_marta.desc: A tourist's good camera in a leather case, left behind in a cupboard at Casa Vicens.

camera.name: Old spare camera
camera.desc: Marta's old spare camera. With it on you, you can take a picture anytime.

postcard.name: Postcard from home
postcard.desc: A postcard of the Botanical Garden in Giessen. On the back, Mama's neat hand: 'Eat properly. Call on Sundays. We are proud of you.'

umbrella.name: Umbrella
umbrella.desc: A sturdy striped umbrella from the UPF lost-and-found. In Barcelona it will mostly be a walking stick.

diploma.name: UPF Diploma of Economics
diploma.desc: The Universitat Pompeu Fabra Diploma of Economics, awarded to Sandra. Rolled, ribboned, and entirely earned.

sundress.name: Yellow sun dress
sundress.desc: Sandra's yellow sun dress, soft cotton the colour of lemon ice cream. For days that insist on being good.

sailor.name: Navy sailor jacket
sailor.desc: Alice's navy sailor jacket with white piping and brass buttons. Makes anyone look like they own a boat.

jersey.name: Blaugrana jersey
jersey.desc: Alba's blue-and-claret FC Barcelona shirt. Wearing it in this city makes strangers nod at you.

festshirt.name: Red festival shirt
festshirt.desc: Alessandra's red festival shirt, the kind worn to La Mercè for the correfoc. A little scorched at one cuff.

barretina.name: Barretina
barretina.desc: Maria's red barretina, the traditional Catalan wool cap. It flops to one side with great dignity.

note1.name: Study Notes 1: Supply & Demand
note1.desc: Chapter 1 of the legendary UPF study guide: supply, demand and the magic of equilibrium. Photocopied so often the margins have gone grey.

note2.name: Study Notes 2: Opportunity Cost
note2.desc: Chapter 2 of the legendary UPF study guide: the true price of everything, including a day at the beach. Maria's own copy, colour-coded.

note3.name: Study Notes 3: The Economics of the Grid
note3.desc: Chapter 3 of the legendary UPF study guide: land, public space and Cerdà's chamfered blocks. Slightly chewed. Retrieved by a very good dog.

note4.name: Study Notes 4: Incentives & the Deposit Bottle
note4.desc: Chapter 4 of the legendary UPF study guide: why people do what they do, explained with a single empty bottle. Found pressed in a paperback.

note5.name: Study Notes 5: Comparative Advantage
note5.desc: Chapter 5 of the legendary UPF study guide: why fishermen should fish and bakers should bake. Faintly salty. Blown in on the sea wind.

bk_history.name: Barcelona: Two Thousand Years in a Hurry
bk_history.desc: A brisk, sardonic history of the city, from Roman walls to Olympic beaches. Dog-eared at the bit about 1714.
bk_history.author: Montserrat Puig i Ferrer

bk_cerda.name: The Man Who Drew the Grid: A Life of Ildefons Cerdà
bk_cerda.desc: A careful biography of the engineer who invented the Eixample, and the word 'urbanisation'. Pencil notes in the margins.
bk_cerda.author: Joaquim Serrallonga

bk_phrase.name: German–Catalan Phrasebook for the Nervous Traveller
bk_phrase.desc: Deutsch–Katalanisch, with fussy footnotes and a great deal of affection. Several phrases are underlined twice.
bk_phrase.author: Dr. Hildegard Oberhuber

bk_valencia.name: València: A Traveller's Companion
bk_valencia.desc: A sunny guide to Catalonia's southern neighbour: oranges, fire, rice and light. The last page seems to wink at you.
bk_valencia.author: Vicent Albors

bk_gaudi.name: Gaudí: A Walking Guide
bk_gaudi.desc: Seven buildings, one pair of comfortable shoes, and a great deal of looking up. A tram ticket marks the chapter on the Sagrada Família.
bk_gaudi.author: Núria Casademunt

bk_santjordi.name: Roses and Dragons: The Book of Sant Jordi
bk_santjordi.desc: The story of Catalonia's most romantic day — books, roses, a very unlucky dragon — with original poems.
bk_santjordi.author: Mercè Rovira

bk_liceu.name: The Liceu: Fire, Bombs and Bel Canto
bk_liceu.desc: A breathless history of Barcelona's opera house on La Rambla. Includes a diagram of the fifth-floor seats where the true fans sit.
bk_liceu.author: Josep Maria Bassas

bk_econ.name: Economics on the Back of a Napkin
bk_econ.desc: An economics primer written, the author claims, entirely in cafés. Diagrams drawn in coffee rings.
bk_econ.author: Prof. Emili Vidal-Roca

bk_med.name: The Middle Sea: An Essay
bk_med.desc: A long, meditative essay on the Mediterranean. Sandy between the pages, as if read on the beach.
bk_med.author: Lluís Ferrater

bk_picasso.name: Picasso's Barcelona Years
bk_picasso.desc: How a teenage prodigy from Málaga became an artist in the streets of Barcelona. Postcard of Els Quatre Gats tucked inside.
bk_picasso.author: Anna Maria Soler

bk_catalan.name: Catalan in Twelve Easy Lessons (and One Hard One)
bk_catalan.desc: A patient, encouraging language guide. The thirteenth lesson has coffee stains and a small sad face drawn beside it.
bk_catalan.author: Pere Casals

bk_cookbook.name: Cuina! A Catalan Kitchen
bk_cookbook.desc: A grandmother's cookbook: warm, bossy, and not open to negotiation. Olive-oil fingerprints on every page.
bk_cookbook.author: Àvia Roser Pujol

bk_barca.name: Més que un club: A History of FC Barcelona
bk_barca.desc: The story of Barça, from a newspaper advert to the Camp Nou. Somebody has pencilled 'VISCA!' on the title page.
bk_barca.author: Jordi Sabaté

bk_gametheory.name: Games People Play at Dinner: A Game Theory Primer
bk_gametheory.desc: An introduction to strategic thinking, illustrated with restaurants, flatmates and one unfortunate paella.
bk_gametheory.author: Dr. Marta Solsona

bk_erasmus.name: Erasmus: How Europe Learned to Share Its Students
bk_erasmus.desc: A warm history of the exchange programme that sent Sandra here. Someone has underlined 'a million babies' and added an exclamation mark.
bk_erasmus.author: Hanne Vermeulen

bk_montserrat.name: Montserrat: The Serrated Mountain
bk_montserrat.desc: A gentle, humorous book about the holy mountain west of Barcelona, written by a monk who clearly enjoys the view.
bk_montserrat.author: Fra Benet Aymerich

bk_ghost.name: The Bookseller's Ghost
bk_ghost.desc: A slim gothic novel bound in faded green cloth. Ponç of Llibreria El Drac has hunted for this very edition for years.
bk_ghost.author: Elvira Quintana i Font

bk_cava.name: Bubbles and Bones: Cava and the Wines of Catalonia
bk_cava.desc: A cheerful guide to Catalan wine, from cava cellars to steep slate vineyards. Smells faintly of cork.
bk_cava.author: Pau Ribalta

bk_camino.name: The Long Way to Santiago
bk_camino.desc: A pilgrim's memoir and guide to the Camino de Santiago. The cover is embossed with a scallop shell.
bk_camino.author: Maite Echeverría

bk_eu.name: Twenty-Seven Chairs: The Story of the European Union
bk_eu.desc: A clear, even-handed history of the EU, from coal and steel to the euro. Surprisingly gripping.
bk_eu.author: Ingrid Vandersteen

bk_atlas.name: A Pocket Atlas of Improbable Places
bk_atlas.desc: A small, delightful book of geographical oddities. Several of the maps are hand-coloured.
bk_atlas.author: Gerard Mas i Font

lb_japan.name: The Island Chain: A History of Japan
lb_japan.desc: A lucid history of Japan from Jōmon pottery to bullet trains. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_japan.author: Kenji Aoyama Serra

lb_china.name: The Middle Kingdom: Four Thousand Years of China
lb_china.desc: A sweeping, readable history of China. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_china.author: Li Wen & Jaume Cortés

lb_india.name: Rivers and Empires: A History of India
lb_india.desc: A history of the Indian subcontinent from Harappa to the present. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_india.author: Priya Raman Vidal

lb_egypt.name: Gift of the Nile: Ancient Egypt
lb_egypt.desc: Pyramids, pharaohs and papyrus: an accessible history of ancient Egypt. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_egypt.author: Dr. Amira Haddad

lb_rome.name: SPQR and the Rest of Us: A History of Rome
lb_rome.desc: The rise and fall of Rome, written with a soft spot for Barcino. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_rome.author: Marc Valls Tarradellas

lb_vikings.name: Longships and Law-Speakers: The Viking Age
lb_vikings.desc: Raiders, traders and poets of the North. Contains no horned helmets whatsoever. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_vikings.author: Ingrid Solheim Puig

lb_mexico.name: The Eagle on the Cactus: A History of Mexico
lb_mexico.desc: From maize to murals: a vivid history of Mexico. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_mexico.author: Ximena Robles i Prat

lb_brazil.name: A Country Named After a Tree: A History of Brazil
lb_brazil.desc: Sugar, gold, samba and a capital built from scratch. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_brazil.author: Rafael Teixeira Soler

lb_germany.name: The Restless Middle: A History of Germany
lb_germany.desc: A sober, humane history of the lands at the heart of Europe. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_germany.author: Katrin Albrecht

lb_italy.name: A Boot Full of Cities: A History of Italy
lb_italy.desc: From city-states to a republic, with frequent pauses for lunch. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_italy.author: Giulia Ferraro Mas

lb_england.name: Rain, Rights and Revolutions: A History of England
lb_england.desc: An affectionate history of England from 1066 to the Industrial Revolution. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_england.author: Oliver Pemberton-Soler

lb_sweden.name: Light in the North: A History of Sweden
lb_sweden.desc: Kings, a sinking warship and the right to roam. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_sweden.author: Astrid Lindqvist Roca

lb_silkroad.name: Threads Across the World: The Silk Roads
lb_silkroad.desc: Silk, paper, faith and plague on the great trade routes of Asia. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_silkroad.author: Farid Nazari & Laia Grau

lb_coldwar.name: The Long Standoff: The Cold War, 1947–1991
lb_coldwar.desc: A clear-eyed account of the four-decade stand-off between East and West. Library copy; do not remove.
lb_coldwar.author: Dr. Tomasz Nowak Pujol

bk_history.title: Barcelona: Two Thousand Years in a Hurry
bk_history.author: Montserrat Puig i Ferrer
bk_history.desc: A brisk, sardonic history of the city, from Roman walls to Olympic beaches. Dog-eared at the bit about 1714.
text: Barcelona began as a small Roman colony with an enormous name: Colonia Iulia Augusta Faventia Paterna Barcino. Founded under Augustus in the last years before the Common Era, it was a tidy grid of streets behind a wall, perched on a low hill the Romans called Mons Taber. Four columns of its Temple of Augustus still stand inside a courtyard on Carrer del Paradís, hidden from the street like a family secret. The city has been hiding its best things in courtyards ever since.

In the Middle Ages the Counts of Barcelona married well and sailed further. The union of 1137, when Count Ramon Berenguer IV was betrothed to Petronila of Aragon, stitched Catalonia into the Crown of Aragon, and Catalan ships went on to trade and fight from Valencia to Sicily, Sardinia and Athens. Merchants paid for Santa Maria del Mar, raised between 1329 and 1383 with astonishing speed; the dockworkers who carried its stones on their backs are carved into its doors. The Llibre del Consolat de Mar, the city's code of sea law, was consulted in ports across the Mediterranean.

Then came the long pause. On 11 September 1714 Barcelona fell to the Bourbon armies of Philip V after a fourteen-month siege, and Catalonia's own institutions were abolished. The day is now the Diada, Catalonia's national day, which tells you a good deal about how the Catalans remember things. The new king built a vast citadel to watch the city, and for a century and a half Barcelona was squeezed inside its medieval walls, becoming one of the most crowded cities in Europe. When the walls finally came down from 1854, the city exhaled into Ildefons Cerdà's great grid.

The twentieth century arrived with exhibitions in 1888 and 1929, bombs, strikes, a civil war and nearly four decades of dictatorship, during which Catalan was pushed out of public life. Democracy returned in the late 1970s, and in 1992 the Olympic Games gave Barcelona the thing it had turned its back on for centuries: its own seafront. Old railway yards and warehouses became beaches and promenades almost overnight. The Romans, one suspects, would have approved of the planning and been baffled by the sunbathing.

bk_cerda.title: The Man Who Drew the Grid: A Life of Ildefons Cerdà
bk_cerda.author: Joaquim Serrallonga
bk_cerda.desc: A careful biography of the engineer who invented the Eixample, and the word 'urbanisation'. Pencil notes in the margins.
text: Ildefons Cerdà was born in 1815 in Centelles, north of Barcelona, and trained as a civil engineer in Madrid, where he learned to love roads, railways and numbers in roughly that order. In 1856 he published a statistical study of the lives of Barcelona's workers — how many lived in a room, how much air they had, how young they died. The figures were appalling, and he never forgot them. Everything he designed afterwards was, in a sense, an answer to that table of numbers.

His plan for the Eixample, the 'Extension' beyond the old walls, was approved by the government in Madrid in 1859, over the head of Barcelona's own council, which had preferred another scheme by the architect Antoni Rovira i Trias. The city never quite forgave him. Cerdà proposed an even grid of blocks about 113 metres on a side, streets twenty metres wide, and — his signature — corners cut off at forty-five degrees, the chamfers or xamfrans, so that carts and, he hoped, steam trams could turn with ease and every crossroads became a small square full of light.

Cerdà imagined blocks built on only two or three sides, with the rest left open as gardens, so that sunlight and breezes could move freely through the city. Speculators had other ideas, and over the following decades most of the blocks were filled in on all four sides, their gardens swallowed by workshops and car parks. In recent years the city has been slowly opening those courtyards again, one 'interior d'illa' at a time.

In 1867 he published his General Theory of Urbanisation, and in doing so coined the word urbanización itself — he is generally credited as the man who named the discipline. He died in 1876, in debt and largely unthanked, while the grid he had drawn was still filling up with the most beautiful buildings in Europe. Walk any street of the Eixample at noon and look at the light pooling on the chamfered corners. That is his signature, and it is written in sunshine.

bk_phrase.title: German–Catalan Phrasebook for the Nervous Traveller
bk_phrase.author: Dr. Hildegard Oberhuber
bk_phrase.desc: Deutsch–Katalanisch, with fussy footnotes and a great deal of affection. Several phrases are underlined twice.
text: Dear reader, you are in Catalonia. Please do not panic. People here speak both Catalan and Spanish, and they will switch between them mid-sentence, sometimes mid-word, with the calm of a tram changing tracks. Begin, as all civilised exchanges begin, with a greeting: 'Bon dia' (good day) until lunch, 'Bona tarda' (good afternoon) until it is properly dark, and 'Bona nit' (good night) only when you truly mean to leave. Saying 'Bona nit' at seven in the evening is not rude, merely optimistic.

Essential phrases, in order of importance. 'Si us plau' — please; use it generously. 'Moltes gràcies' — thank you very much; the double 'moltes' costs nothing. 'Perdoni' — excuse me, for squeezing past someone on a crowded bus. 'On és...?' — where is...?, followed by pointing hopefully. 'Quant costa?' — how much is it?, to be asked before, not after, you have eaten the thing. And my personal favourite, 'Déu n'hi do', which means roughly 'goodness, that's quite something' and is suitable for sunsets, prices and other people's children.

A note on time. In Germany, dinner at nine o'clock in the evening is a scandal. In Barcelona it is early. Lunch is the main meal and rarely begins before two; restaurants may look empty and puzzled at seven. Do not take this personally. Before you eat, someone will say 'Bon profit!' — enjoy your meal — and the correct response is to say it back, with feeling. At a café, order 'un tallat' if you would like a small coffee with a splash of milk. It is the most reasonable drink in Europe.

Finally, greetings with the face. Friends and new acquaintances often exchange two kisses, one on each cheek, even at the first meeting. Lean in gently and do not collide noses; if in doubt, follow the other person's lead and trust in providence. Catalans value 'seny', calm good sense, and 'rauxa', sudden glorious madness, in roughly equal measure. You, dear reader, brought the seny. Allow the city to supply the rauxa. Viel Glück!

bk_valencia.title: València: A Traveller's Companion
bk_valencia.author: Vicent Albors
bk_valencia.desc: A sunny guide to Catalonia's southern neighbour: oranges, fire, rice and light. The last page seems to wink at you.
text: València is a city that smells of orange blossom in spring and gunpowder in March, and is unembarrassed by either. It sits three hundred and fifty kilometres down the coast from Barcelona, among the huerta, the fertile irrigated fields that have fed it since the Moors laid out their channels a thousand years ago. The Tribunal de les Aigües, the Water Court, still meets every Thursday at noon outside the cathedral door to settle irrigation disputes, as it has for centuries, speaking in Valencian and keeping no written records. It is said to be the oldest court in Europe still sitting.

In 1957 the river Túria burst its banks and flooded the city, so the Valencians did something magnificent: they moved the river. The old riverbed, curving right through the heart of town, became a nine-kilometre park of orange trees, football pitches, fountains and cycle paths. At its seaward end rises Santiago Calatrava's City of Arts and Sciences, white and skeletal, like an ocean liner that has decided to become a whale. Bring sunglasses; the architecture is extremely bright.

Every March the city holds Les Falles. For weeks, enormous satirical sculptures of wood, cardboard and papier-mâché — some taller than the houses around them — fill the squares, and on the night of 19 March, the feast of Saint Joseph, nearly all of them are set on fire. UNESCO added the festival to its list of intangible heritage in 2016. At two o'clock every afternoon of the festival, the mascletà shakes the Plaça de l'Ajuntament with firecrackers so loud they rearrange your ribs.

Eat paella at lunchtime, never at dinner, and eat the proper kind — rabbit, chicken, flat green beans, saffron, and rice from the Albufera lagoon just south of town. Drink orxata, cold and sweet, made from tiger nuts, and dunk a long soft farton pastry into it. Then, my friend, take the coast road south from Barcelona. The bridge over the river will surely be open any day now. Surely. Until then, this book will have to do.

bk_gaudi.title: Gaudí: A Walking Guide
bk_gaudi.author: Núria Casademunt
bk_gaudi.desc: Seven buildings, one pair of comfortable shoes, and a great deal of looking up. A tram ticket marks the chapter on the Sagrada Família.
text: Antoni Gaudí was born in 1852 in or near Reus, the son of a coppersmith, and he claimed that watching his father hammer curved sheets of metal taught him to think in three dimensions. When he graduated in architecture in 1878, the director of the school is reported to have said that they had given the title either to a madman or to a genius — time would tell. Time has told. Start this walk early, wear flat shoes, and remember to look up; Gaudí rarely put his best ideas at eye level.

Begin at Casa Vicens, his first major house, finished in 1885: green and white tiles, yellow marigolds, turrets with Moorish airs. Walk south to the Passeig de Gràcia for Casa Batlló, remodelled in 1904–1906, where the balconies look like masks or bones and the roof arches like the back of a dragon. A few blocks up stands Casa Milà, 'La Pedrera', its stone façade rippling like the sea cliff it was meant to evoke. Visit the roof to meet the chimneys, which look very much like helmeted sentries and are rumoured to have inspired a certain film villain.

Gaudí distrusted straight lines — 'the straight line belongs to men, the curve belongs to God', he is often quoted as saying. He designed his arches by hanging weighted chains from the ceiling of his workshop and photographing them upside down; a hanging chain makes a perfect catenary curve, and turned the right way up, that curve stands by itself. He decorated with trencadís, a mosaic of broken tiles and plates, which is thrifty, dazzling, and the reason every Barcelona gift shop now sells lizards.

End at the Sagrada Família, where he worked for forty-three years and is buried in the crypt. In June 1926, walking to Mass, he was struck by a tram on the Gran Via; poorly dressed and carrying no identification, he was at first taken for a beggar and received only basic care. He died three days later. Seven of his works are now UNESCO World Heritage sites. He would probably have been quietly pleased, and then gone straight back to work on the towers.

bk_santjordi.title: Roses and Dragons: The Book of Sant Jordi
bk_santjordi.author: Mercè Rovira
bk_santjordi.desc: The story of Catalonia's most romantic day — books, roses, a very unlucky dragon — with original poems.
text: On 23 April, Catalonia's patron saint's day, Barcelona becomes a single enormous bookshop. Stalls line La Rambla and the Passeig de Gràcia, authors sign until their wrists ache, and millions of roses change hands. The old custom was that men gave women a rose and women gave men a book; nowadays everyone gives everyone both, which is much more sensible. Since 1995 the date has also been UNESCO's World Book and Copyright Day, chosen because Cervantes and Shakespeare both died in April 1616 — though not, strictly speaking, on the same day.

The legend is set, in the most popular Catalan telling, in the town of Montblanc. A dragon terrorised the countryside and was appeased with a daily victim chosen by lot, until the lot fell upon the princess. A knight named Jordi rode in, drove his lance through the beast, and from its spilled blood grew a rose bush, from which he picked a flower for the princess. It is a violent story with a surprisingly gentle ending, which is very Catalan.

Here is a small poem, written for the day.

  On Sant Jordi
  The dragon never read a book —
  that was his first mistake.
  He never smelled a single rose,
  he never learned to wait.
  So give me pages, give me thorns,
  the long queue and the crowd:
  a city that has learned to love
  by reading it aloud.

And one more, shorter, for anyone who has ever stood on the Rambla at dusk on the twenty-third, holding a flower in one hand and a new novel in the other.

  Paper and petal —
  one will fade by Sunday,
  one will keep you up all night.

Choose your book the way you choose your rose: slowly, by its scent, and for someone who will open it.

bk_liceu.title: The Liceu: Fire, Bombs and Bel Canto
bk_liceu.author: Josep Maria Bassas
bk_liceu.desc: A breathless history of Barcelona's opera house on La Rambla. Includes a diagram of the fifth-floor seats where the true fans sit.
text: The Gran Teatre del Liceu opened on La Rambla in 1847, built not by a king but by subscribers, which is why Barcelona's opera house has always felt like it belongs to the city rather than a court. It was among the largest opera houses in Europe, with more than two thousand seats rising in horseshoe tiers of red and gold. The aristocracy sat in the boxes; the true fanatics climbed to the fifth floor, where the tickets were cheapest and the shouting loudest.

Opera loves a tragedy, and the Liceu has had several. In 1861 fire gutted the building, and it was rebuilt within a year. On 7 November 1893, during a performance of Rossini's William Tell, an anarchist named Santiago Salvador threw two bombs from the upper tiers into the stalls; one exploded, killing some twenty people. For years afterwards, it is said, the seats where the victims had fallen were left empty.

On 31 January 1994, during repair work, a spark set the stage curtain alight, and within hours the auditorium was destroyed. The whole city seemed to go into mourning. Rebuilt with public money and private donations, faithful to the old horseshoe but with modern machinery beneath, the Liceu reopened in October 1999 with Puccini's Turandot, and the audience wept in their brand-new seats.

Barcelona has given the world two of its great voices: the soprano Montserrat Caballé, born in the city in 1933, and the tenor Josep Carreras, born in 1946, both of whom sang at the Liceu long before the world knew their names. Go to a performance if you can. Buy a cheap seat on the fifth floor, lean over the rail, and listen to the house breathe in before the first note.

bk_econ.title: Economics on the Back of a Napkin
bk_econ.author: Prof. Emili Vidal-Roca
bk_econ.desc: An economics primer written, the author claims, entirely in cafés. Diagrams drawn in coffee rings.
text: Economics is the study of how people choose when they cannot have everything — which is to say, it is the study of people. There are only so many hours in a day, euros in a wallet and croissants in the basket at nine in the morning. This condition is called scarcity, and it is not a problem to be solved but a fact to be managed. Every choice therefore has a cost, measured not only in money but in whatever else you might have done instead.

Economists think 'at the margin'. The question is rarely 'coffee or no coffee in my life?' but 'one more coffee, right now?' The first coffee of the morning is a small miracle; the fourth is merely a tremor. As we consume more of something, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit tends to fall — diminishing marginal utility, in the jargon. This is why nobody queues for the fourth croissant.

People respond to incentives. Put a one-euro deposit on a glass bottle and bottles stop appearing in the gutter; tax something and you tend to get less of it; pay people per piece and they will work faster, if not always better. The art of economic policy lies largely in predicting how people will respond to a rule, rather than assuming they will obey it gratefully.

Finally, trade makes both sides better off, or they would not trade. When the baker sells you bread, you value the loaf more than your two euros, and the baker values your two euros more than the loaf. Two people, each slightly richer than before, and nobody lost. Scribble that on a napkin, leave a tip, and you have understood more economics than many people who shout about it on television.

bk_med.title: The Middle Sea: An Essay
bk_med.author: Lluís Ferrater
bk_med.desc: A long, meditative essay on the Mediterranean. Sandy between the pages, as if read on the beach.
text: The Mediterranean is almost a lake. At the Strait of Gibraltar it narrows to about fourteen kilometres, and through that slender door the Atlantic pours in to replace what the hot sun takes out, for this sea loses more water to evaporation than its rivers can bring it. It is saltier than the ocean and nearly tideless; on the beach at Barcelona, the difference between high and low water is a matter of a few centimetres, which is why the Catalans have never had to learn to fear the moon.

Around six million years ago the door closed. Geologists call it the Messinian salinity crisis: cut off from the Atlantic, the sea largely dried out, leaving basins of salt more than a kilometre thick, now buried beneath the seabed. Then, about five and a third million years ago, the Atlantic broke through again, and — so one theory goes — the refilling may have been swift, a flood beyond imagining. Every time you swim here, you are floating in the second attempt.

Around its shores grew the triad of wheat, olive and vine, which gave a hundred peoples bread, oil and wine, and gave them, in turn, a common table. The historian Fernand Braudel wrote that the Mediterranean was not one sea but a succession of seas, a crossroads of civilisations rather than a border between them. Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Catalans and Venetians all sailed it, traded on it, fought on it, and left their words in each other's mouths.

Sit on the sand at dusk and the sea turns the colour of a ripe plum, and every culture that ever stood here has had a word for that moment. I think this is the Mediterranean's real gift: not its beauty, which is considerable, but its insistence that people who arrive from elsewhere are, sooner or later, simply neighbours. Walk into it up to your knees. Let it tell you where you are.

bk_picasso.title: Picasso's Barcelona Years
bk_picasso.author: Anna Maria Soler
bk_picasso.desc: How a teenage prodigy from Málaga became an artist in the streets of Barcelona. Postcard of Els Quatre Gats tucked inside.
text: Pablo Ruiz Picasso arrived in Barcelona in 1895, aged thirteen, when his father, the painter José Ruiz Blasco, took a teaching post at La Llotja, the city's school of fine arts. The boy sat the entrance examination for the advanced classes and, according to family legend, completed in a day what candidates were allowed a month to do. The story has been polished by retelling, but the drawings survive, and they are frighteningly good.

At fifteen he painted Science and Charity, a large, sombre canvas of a doctor and a nun at a sick woman's bedside, which won an honourable mention at the national exhibition in Madrid. He was, in other words, already an accomplished academic painter — and he would spend the rest of his life dismantling that accomplishment, piece by deliberate piece, to see what lay beneath.

In Barcelona he found the city's avant-garde gathered at Els Quatre Gats, a tavern in the old town modelled on the cabarets of Paris. In February 1900 he held his first solo exhibition on its walls, mostly portraits of his friends, and he designed the cover of its menu. Between trips to Paris, the grief of his friend Casagemas's suicide drove him into his Blue Period, much of it painted in Barcelona: thin figures, cold light, beggars and mothers in a world of blue.

He left for Paris for good in 1904, but Barcelona followed him. Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, the 1907 painting that cracked modern art open, takes its name, many believe, from Carrer d'Avinyó, a street near the port he knew well. In 1963 the Museu Picasso opened in a row of medieval palaces on Carrer de Montcada, and in 1968 he gave it his fifty-eight variations on Velázquez's Las Meninas. He never returned to see it; under Franco, he refused to set foot in Spain.

bk_catalan.title: Catalan in Twelve Easy Lessons (and One Hard One)
bk_catalan.author: Pere Casals
bk_catalan.desc: A patient, encouraging language guide. The thirteenth lesson has coffee stains and a small sad face drawn beside it.
text: Catalan is a Romance language, descended from the Latin spoken by the Roman soldiers and settlers of the north-eastern Iberian peninsula, and it is spoken today by around ten million people. You will hear it in Catalonia, in Valencia (where it is called Valencian), in the Balearic Islands, in the Principality of Andorra — where it is the sole official language — in the Roussillon across the French border, and even in the Sardinian city of l'Alguer. It is not a dialect of Spanish, and nobody will thank you for suggesting so.

Modern written Catalan owes a great deal to Pompeu Fabra, an engineer by training, whose grammar of 1918 and dictionary of 1932 gave the language its standard form. Look out for its most famous character, the 'ela geminada', the dotted double L in words like col·lecció and intel·ligent. It tells you to pronounce both L's, slightly lengthened, and it tells everyone else that you are reading Catalan.

Lessons one to twelve are pleasant. 'Bon dia' for good morning; 'adéu' for goodbye; 'fins demà' for see you tomorrow; 'gràcies' for thanks. Numbers: un, dos, tres, quatre. The days: dilluns, dimarts, dimecres, dijous, divendres, dissabte, diumenge. Food: pa (bread), aigua (water), vi (wine), formatge (cheese). You will be ordering lunch within a week and understanding the reply within a month.

Lesson thirteen concerns the weak pronouns 'en' and 'hi', which replace entire phrases and appear in places no reasonable person would expect them. 'N'hi ha' means 'there is some of it there'. 'Ens n'hi anem' means, roughly, 'we are leaving from there to somewhere'. Native speakers use them flawlessly and cannot explain them. Do not despair. Nod, smile, and say 'Déu n'hi do' — it fits almost everywhere.

bk_cookbook.title: Cuina! A Catalan Kitchen
bk_cookbook.author: Àvia Roser Pujol
bk_cookbook.desc: A grandmother's cookbook: warm, bossy, and not open to negotiation. Olive-oil fingerprints on every page.
text: Before we start, wash your hands and listen. Catalan cooking stands on two pillars: the sofregit at the beginning and the picada at the end. The sofregit is onion cooked slowly in olive oil until it is soft and golden and sweet, then tomato, then patience — forty minutes, not ten, and I don't care what the television says. The picada is crushed in a mortar at the end: almonds or hazelnuts, garlic, parsley, sometimes a little fried bread, stirred into the pot to thicken and perfume it. Between the two, you may cook almost anything.

Pa amb tomàquet. You will think this is too simple to write down. It is not. Take good bread, toasted or not, as you like. Cut a very ripe tomato in half and rub it into the bread firmly until the crumb is pink and the skin is almost empty in your hand. Add a thread of olive oil and a pinch of salt. That is all. If I see you putting the tomato on in slices, like a sandwich, we will have words.

Allioli means 'garlic and oil', and in the old way that is all it is: garlic crushed to a paste in a mortar with salt, then oil added drop by drop while you turn the pestle in one direction, never the other, until it holds together like a thick cream. It takes time and a strong arm, and it will fail the first three times. Do not, under any circumstances, reach for a blender and an egg and call it allioli. I will know.

Crema catalana, for Sant Josep on 19 March, or for any day you deserve it. Warm a litre of milk with the peel of a lemon and a stick of cinnamon. Whisk six egg yolks with sugar and a spoon of cornflour, pour in the milk, and stir over a low flame until it coats the spoon. Chill it in shallow dishes. Just before serving, cover it with sugar and burn it with a hot iron until it is glassy. Then tap it with your spoon, listen to the crack, and think of me.

bk_barca.title: Més que un club: A History of FC Barcelona
bk_barca.author: Jordi Sabaté
bk_barca.desc: The story of Barça, from a newspaper advert to the Camp Nou. Somebody has pencilled 'VISCA!' on the title page.
text: It began with a small advertisement. In October 1899 a young Swiss accountant named Hans Gamper — later Catalanised as Joan Gamper — placed a notice in the sports magazine Los Deportes, looking for people who wanted to play football. On 29 November, a dozen men met at a gymnasium and founded the Futbol Club Barcelona. Gamper went on to be player, president and patron, and the club still plays a pre-season trophy in his name every summer.

The famous blue and deep red — blaugrana — have a disputed origin, and every theory has its partisans; one says Gamper borrowed the colours of his old Swiss club, another credits the Comas brothers and their school colours. What is not disputed is the club's place in the city's story. During the long Franco dictatorship, when Catalan was pushed out of public life, the stadium became one of the few places where tens of thousands could gather and speak it aloud. In 1968 president Narcís de Carreras gave the club its motto: 'més que un club' — more than a club.

The Camp Nou opened in 1957 and grew into one of the largest stadiums in Europe. Johan Cruyff arrived as a player in 1973 and returned as coach in 1988 to build the 'Dream Team', which won the club's first European Cup at Wembley in 1992. His ideas — possession, movement, the ball as the thing that does the running — reshaped the club's academy, La Masia, and through it football across the world.

La Masia produced a generation of players who passed the ball as if it were a secret, and the club signed a small, shy thirteen-year-old from Rosario named Lionel Messi in 2000. He would stay twenty-one years. The club is owned by its members, the socis, who elect its president, which means that on a matchday the person beside you in the stands may, in a small way, own the place. Sing along. Nobody will check your accent.

bk_gametheory.title: Games People Play at Dinner: A Game Theory Primer
bk_gametheory.author: Dr. Marta Solsona
bk_gametheory.desc: An introduction to strategic thinking, illustrated with restaurants, flatmates and one unfortunate paella.
text: Game theory is the study of situations in which what is best for me depends on what you do, and what is best for you depends on what I do. That describes chess, but also traffic, auctions, climate treaties and deciding who washes up. A 'game' here simply means a situation with players, choices and payoffs. Nobody has to be having fun, and frequently nobody is.

The most famous game is the Prisoner's Dilemma. Two suspects are questioned separately. If both stay silent, both get a short sentence; if both confess, both get a medium one; but if one confesses and the other stays silent, the confessor walks free and the silent one gets the longest sentence of all. Each, reasoning alone, does better by confessing whatever the other does — and so both confess, and both end up worse off than if they had trusted each other. It is a tragedy in four boxes.

In 1950 John Nash described the kind of outcome we just found: a situation in which no player can do better by changing their own choice alone. We call it a Nash equilibrium. It is not necessarily good, fair or wise; it is merely stable. Think of a group dinner where the bill will be split equally. Each diner, knowing the cost is shared, orders the expensive fish. Everyone pays for everyone's fish, and the equilibrium is a very large bill.

Happily, most of life is a repeated game. In 1980 the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran a tournament in which computer programs played the Prisoner's Dilemma against each other hundreds of times. The winner was one of the simplest: Tit for Tat, which cooperates first and then copies whatever its opponent did last time. Be nice, retaliate, forgive, be clear. As advice for flatmates, it is hard to beat.

bk_erasmus.title: Erasmus: How Europe Learned to Share Its Students
bk_erasmus.author: Hanne Vermeulen
bk_erasmus.desc: A warm history of the exchange programme that sent Sandra here. Someone has underlined 'a million babies' and added an exclamation mark.
text: The programme is named after Erasmus of Rotterdam, the great Renaissance scholar, born around 1466, who studied and taught in Paris, Leuven, Cambridge, Basel and Turin and wrote to friends across the continent in Latin, the common tongue of educated Europe. It is also, conveniently, an acronym: the EuRopean Community Action Scheme for the Mobility of University Students. Civil servants love a good acronym almost as much as scholars love a good footnote.

The idea had been championed for years, most tirelessly by the Italian educator Sofia Corradi — affectionately known as 'Mamma Erasmus' — who had studied in New York as a young woman and returned to find that Italy would not recognise her exams. The European Community launched the programme in 1987. In that first academic year, 3,244 students from eleven countries packed their suitcases and set off to study somewhere they could barely pronounce.

Since then, many millions of people have taken part in the programme and its successors. Studies suggest that former Erasmus students are markedly more likely to work abroad, to speak several languages and to have a partner from another country. In 2014 a study for the European Commission estimated that around a million babies had been born to couples who met on Erasmus. It is, among other things, the most successful dating agency in European history.

Barcelona has always been one of the most popular destinations, and in 2002 it became the setting of Cédric Klapisch's film L'Auberge espagnole, about a French student sharing a chaotic Eixample flat with housemates from half of Europe. Every Erasmus student recognises it: the misunderstood rules of the fridge, the phone calls home, the moment you realise that you now think in two languages. You arrive a visitor. You leave with a second hometown and a slightly different accent in both.

bk_montserrat.title: Montserrat: The Serrated Mountain
bk_montserrat.author: Fra Benet Aymerich
bk_montserrat.desc: A gentle, humorous book about the holy mountain west of Barcelona, written by a monk who clearly enjoys the view.
text: About fifty kilometres north-west of Barcelona, a mountain rises from the plain as though someone had set down a row of enormous stone fingers and forgotten to pick them up. Its name means 'serrated mountain', and the Catalans say it was sawn into shape by angels. Geologists, who are less poetic, explain that it is made of conglomerate — pebbles and sand cemented together on the floor of an ancient river delta — which the weather has carved into these pink, rounded towers over many millions of years.

Our Benedictine monastery was founded in the eleventh century, in 1025, and has been destroyed, rebuilt, burned by Napoleon's troops and rebuilt again. Its heart is La Moreneta, 'the little dark one', a Romanesque statue of the Virgin and Child blackened by age and candle smoke, who is the patron saint of Catalonia. Pilgrims queue to touch the orb in her hand. I have watched thousands of them do it, and I have never once seen anyone look disappointed afterwards.

Our boys' choir, the Escolania, is one of the oldest in Europe, documented since the fourteenth century, and sings most days in the basilica. You may arrive by the rack railway or by the cable car, the Aeri, which has swung visitors up the cliff since 1930; I recommend the train, as it gives you time to pray. The highest summit, Sant Jeroni, stands at 1,236 metres, and on a clear day you can see the Pyrenees, the sea and, some claim, Mallorca.

Some say that Montserrat inspired the legend of Montsalvat, the mountain of the Holy Grail, and that Wagner himself had it in mind. I cannot confirm this, and the Rule of Saint Benedict discourages gossip. What I can tell you is this: stand on the path above the monastery at dusk, when the rock turns rose and gold and the valley fills with shadow, and you will understand why people have been climbing up here for a thousand years to say thank you.

bk_ghost.title: The Bookseller's Ghost
bk_ghost.author: Elvira Quintana i Font
bk_ghost.desc: A slim gothic novel bound in faded green cloth. Ponç of Llibreria El Drac has hunted for this very edition for years.
text: The shop on Carrer de la Palla had been closed for eleven years when Clara Vives inherited the key. It hung on a ribbon the colour of old blood, and the notary handed it over as though glad to be rid of it. Inside, the air tasted of paper and candle wax. The shelves ran up into darkness, and every book stood spine out, dignified, in perfect alphabetical order — which was strange, because her great-uncle Anselm had been dead for eleven years, and the dust lay thick on everything except the books.

On the first night she heard the ladder. It rolled along its brass rail with a sound like a long sigh, stopped, and rolled again. In the morning a single volume lay on the counter, open at the title page: Tirant lo Blanc, Valencia, a printing she did not know existed. On the second night the ladder rolled until dawn, and in the morning there were three books on the counter, and a note in brown ink in a hand she recognised from birthday cards received long ago: 'These are not for sale.'

Clara was a practical woman who had come to sell the stock and the lease and return to Girona before the summer. She wrote a notice for the window — ALL BOOKS HALF PRICE — and taped it to the glass. In the morning the notice lay on the floor, folded into a neat paper boat, and every book that had been shelved within reach of the door had moved to the very top of the highest shelves, where no customer could possibly reach them.

She sat up the third night in the reading chair with a candle and a bottle of wine, and at a quarter past three the ladder began to roll. In the dim light she saw it clearly: an old man in a cardigan, thin as a bookmark, climbing slowly, running a finger along the spines as if counting them. 'Oncle Anselm,' she said, and he turned, and his face was sad and very kind. 'Every one of these,' he said, in a voice like pages turning, 'was chosen for somebody. Some of them are still waiting for their person.'

Clara did not sell the shop. She opened it at ten each morning and closed it when the light went, and when customers asked for something, she learned to wait before answering, listening for the faint roll of the ladder behind her. Sometimes a book would be lying on the counter when she turned around. It was always the right one. People said the shop on Carrer de la Palla had the best bookseller in Barcelona, and Clara, who knew better, said nothing at all — except, now and then, late at night, 'Gràcies, oncle.'

bk_cava.title: Bubbles and Bones: Cava and the Wines of Catalonia
bk_cava.author: Pau Ribalta
bk_cava.desc: A cheerful guide to Catalan wine, from cava cellars to steep slate vineyards. Smells faintly of cork.
text: In 1872 Josep Raventós of the Codorníu estate in Sant Sadurní d'Anoia made the first bottles of Catalan sparkling wine by the traditional method, in which a second fermentation takes place inside the bottle itself. The town, forty-odd kilometres west of Barcelona, sits on kilometres of underground cellars where millions of bottles rest in the dark, and it remains the heart of cava country today. The name 'cava' simply means 'cellar'.

The classic blend uses three native white grapes: Macabeu for freshness, Xarel·lo for body and backbone, and Parellada for a floral lightness. After the second fermentation the yeast sediment is coaxed down into the neck of each bottle by turning it a little at a time — a task once done entirely by hand — then frozen and expelled with a soft pop. Catalans drink cava at every celebration, and at quite a few ordinary Tuesdays.

In the late nineteenth century the vine pest phylloxera, which had already ravaged France, reached Catalonia from 1879 and destroyed most of its vineyards. Growers replanted on resistant American rootstocks, and many chose white grapes suited to sparkling wine, which is one reason cava flourished. Disaster, as so often in wine, turned out to be a change of direction.

For something darker and deeper, travel south-west to the Priorat, where old vines of Garnatxa and Carinyena cling to terraces of crumbling slate called llicorella. The yields are tiny and the wines intense, and the region is one of only two in Spain, with Rioja, to hold the highest classification of origin. Drink it slowly, with friends, and in no particular hurry.

bk_camino.title: The Long Way to Santiago
bk_camino.author: Maite Echeverría
bk_camino.desc: A pilgrim's memoir and guide to the Camino de Santiago. The cover is embossed with a scallop shell.
text: In the ninth century, the story goes, a hermit following a field of stars found a tomb in Galicia that was declared to be that of the apostle Saint James. A city grew around it, Santiago de Compostela, and for more than a thousand years pilgrims have walked there from all over Europe. They carry a scallop shell, the saint's emblem, tied to their packs; the grooves of the shell, some say, are the many roads meeting at a single point.

The most famous route, the Camino Francés, begins at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port in the French Pyrenees and runs roughly eight hundred kilometres west. Pilgrims carry a credencial, a passport stamped at every hostel, café and church along the way, and to receive the Compostela certificate at the end you must walk at least the last hundred kilometres, or cycle the last two hundred. The routes to Santiago have been UNESCO World Heritage since 1993.

From Barcelona, pilgrims can follow the Catalan Camí de Sant Jaume, which climbs to Montserrat before heading west across Aragon to join the main road. I set out from my own front door with blisters I did not yet know I owned. By the third week I had learned more about my feet, my patience and the kindness of strangers than in the thirty years before.

In the cathedral at Santiago hangs the Botafumeiro, a huge silver censer that is swung across the transept by a team of men hauling on a rope until it flies nearly to the ceiling, trailing incense. Some say it was first swung to freshen the air after crowds of unwashed pilgrims. I prefer to think of it as the cathedral exhaling. When I saw it, I wept, and so did the man from Hamburg next to me, and neither of us was embarrassed.

bk_eu.title: Twenty-Seven Chairs: The Story of the European Union
bk_eu.author: Ingrid Vandersteen
bk_eu.desc: A clear, even-handed history of the EU, from coal and steel to the euro. Surprisingly gripping.
text: On 9 May 1950, five years after the end of the Second World War, the French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed that France and Germany pool their coal and steel under a common authority, so that war between them would become, in his words, 'not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible'. The following year six countries — France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg — signed the Treaty of Paris. The 9th of May is now celebrated as Europe Day.

The Treaty of Rome in 1957 created the European Economic Community, a common market for goods, which grew steadily wider as Britain, Ireland and Denmark joined in 1973 and Greece in 1981. Spain and Portugal, both recently returned to democracy, joined in 1986 — a moment still remembered in Barcelona as the country opening its windows. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the European Union itself and set the path to a single currency.

The euro was launched in 1999 and arrived in pockets on 1 January 2002, with a common side on every coin and a national side chosen by each country. In 2012 the Union was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for having helped to transform most of Europe 'from a continent of war to a continent of peace'. Its critics point to its distance, its bureaucracy and its crises; its admirers point to seventy years without war between its members. Both are worth hearing.

Since the United Kingdom's departure in 2020 there have been twenty-seven member states and twenty-four official languages, including German and Spanish, while Catalan is spoken by millions of its citizens. The Union's motto is 'United in diversity'. In practice this means endless meetings, simultaneous interpretation, and students from Giessen studying economics in Barcelona without a visa — which is, after all, rather the point.

bk_atlas.title: A Pocket Atlas of Improbable Places
bk_atlas.author: Gerard Mas i Font
bk_atlas.desc: A small, delightful book of geographical oddities. Several of the maps are hand-coloured.
text: Between Egypt and Sudan lies a trapezoid of desert called Bir Tawil, about two thousand square kilometres in size, which neither country claims. Thanks to two different border lines drawn in 1899 and 1902, each nation claims the neighbouring Hala'ib Triangle instead, and so Bir Tawil belongs to no one — one of the very few pieces of land on Earth in that condition. It has no people, no water, and a surprising number of would-be kings.

On the Belgian–Dutch border sits the town of Baarle, where the boundary wanders through gardens, shops and living rooms. Belgian enclaves lie inside the Netherlands, and Dutch enclaves lie inside those Belgian enclaves; house numbers carry little flags so that residents know which country their front door is in. Closer to home, the Catalan town of Llívia is a piece of Spain entirely surrounded by France, a few kilometres from the border, thanks to the careful wording of a treaty of 1659 that handed over 'villages' — and Llívia insisted it was a town.

In the river Bidasoa, between Spain and France, floats Pheasant Island, a small wooded island where a royal marriage was arranged in 1659. It is a condominium, jointly ruled: it belongs to Spain for six months of the year and to France for the other six, handed over each time with modest ceremony. There are no pheasants.

Finally, the loneliest point in the sea: Point Nemo, in the South Pacific, is the spot in the ocean farthest from any land, more than 2,600 kilometres from the nearest island. Often the closest humans to it are the astronauts passing overhead on the space station. It is also where old spacecraft are sent to fall and sink. There is a lesson in that somewhere about keeping your distance, but this atlas is too cheerful to find it.

lb_japan.title: The Island Chain: A History of Japan
lb_japan.author: Kenji Aoyama Serra
lb_japan.desc: A lucid history of Japan from Jōmon pottery to bullet trains. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The first people of the Japanese islands left behind some of the oldest pottery on Earth. The Jōmon culture, named after the cord-marked patterns pressed into its clay, made vessels more than fourteen thousand years ago, long before farming reached the islands. Rice cultivation arrived later from the continent, and with it villages, rulers and the slow knitting-together of a state. By the sixth century, Buddhism and Chinese writing had crossed the sea as well, and Japan began adapting both into something recognisably its own.

In the Heian period, from 794, the imperial court at Kyoto produced one of the great literary cultures of the world. Around the year 1000, a lady-in-waiting known to us as Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel: a long, subtle story of love, rank and impermanence at court. Its contemporary, Sei Shōnagon, kept The Pillow Book, a collection of lists and observations — 'Things That Make One's Heart Beat Faster' — that reads today like a very elegant blog.

Real power slipped from the emperor to military rulers, the shoguns, and to the samurai class that served them. After a century of civil war, Tokugawa Ieyasu unified the country and in 1603 founded a shogunate that would last until 1868. For much of that time Japan restricted foreign contact severely, allowing only limited trade, chiefly through the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Behind these closed doors flourished kabuki theatre, woodblock prints and a thriving urban culture in Edo, the city we now call Tokyo.

In 1853 the American commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay with his 'black ships' and demanded that Japan open its ports. The shock toppled the old order. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 returned authority to the emperor and launched one of the most rapid modernisations in history: railways, conscription, a constitution, factories and a navy, all within a generation. It also set Japan on the path of empire and war that ended in catastrophe in 1945, with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

From the ruins came an economic transformation. In 1964, the year Tokyo hosted the Olympic Games, the first Shinkansen bullet train began running between Tokyo and Osaka, and it became a symbol of a nation reborn. Japan today pairs ancient temples with vending machines on remote mountain paths, and it treasures the idea of mono no aware — a gentle awareness of the passing of things. Anyone who has watched the cherry blossom fall in a Barcelona spring will understand it perfectly.

lb_china.title: The Middle Kingdom: Four Thousand Years of China
lb_china.author: Li Wen & Jaume Cortés
lb_china.desc: A sweeping, readable history of China. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The earliest Chinese writing we can read survives on 'oracle bones' of the Shang dynasty, over three thousand years old: turtle shells and ox shoulder-blades inscribed with questions to the ancestors, then heated until they cracked. The king would read the answer in the cracks — will the harvest be good, will the queen's child be healthy, will it rain tomorrow — and scribes carved the result beside the question. Many of the characters on those bones are the direct ancestors of characters written today.

In 221 BC the ruler of the state of Qin conquered his rivals and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He standardised writing, weights, measures and even the width of cart axles, and linked earlier walls into a great defensive line. He was buried with an army of thousands of life-sized terracotta soldiers, each face apparently individual, discovered by farmers digging a well in 1974. His dynasty collapsed within a few years of his death, but the idea of a single China endured.

The Han dynasty that followed gave its name to the majority of the Chinese people, and tradition credits a court official, Cai Lun, with perfecting papermaking in the year 105. Under the Tang, poetry flourished — Li Bai and Du Fu are still memorised by schoolchildren — and the capital, Chang'an, was one of the largest cities in the world. The Song dynasty developed movable type, gunpowder weapons and the magnetic compass, and paid its taxes partly in the world's first government-issued paper money.

Between 1405 and 1433, the Ming admiral Zheng He led seven vast expeditions across the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa, with ships far larger than anything Europe would build for generations. Then the voyages stopped, the records were neglected, and China turned inward. The Qing dynasty, founded by the Manchus in 1644, reached its greatest extent in the eighteenth century, but in the nineteenth it was humiliated by the Opium Wars with Britain and torn by rebellion.

The last emperor abdicated in 1912, after the revolution of 1911. Decades of warlords, invasion and civil war followed, until the Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic in 1949. After the upheavals of the Mao era, reforms from 1978 opened the economy and set off growth that lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, at great speed and with great consequences. The result is a country where very old things and very new things stand, often uneasily, side by side.

lb_india.title: Rivers and Empires: A History of India
lb_india.author: Priya Raman Vidal
lb_india.desc: A history of the Indian subcontinent from Harappa to the present. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Around 2600 BC, along the Indus river in what is now Pakistan and north-western India, arose one of the world's first great urban civilisations. Its cities, Harappa and Mohenjo-daro among them, had carefully planned streets, standardised bricks and weights, and covered drains that many later cities would envy. Its people wrote in a script that we still cannot read. By around 1900 BC the great cities were in decline, perhaps as rivers shifted and the climate changed, and their secrets went quiet under the silt.

In the third century BC the emperor Ashoka of the Maurya dynasty ruled most of the subcontinent. After a bloody conquest of Kalinga, the story goes, he was so horrified by the slaughter that he embraced Buddhism and nonviolence, and had his edicts on justice, tolerance and kindness to animals carved on rocks and pillars across his empire. The lion capital from one of his pillars is now the national emblem of India.

Indian mathematicians gave the world one of its most useful inventions: the decimal place-value system with zero, the ancestor of the numerals we use today. In 628 the astronomer Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers, treating zero as a number in its own right. Carried west by Persian and Arab scholars, these 'Hindu-Arabic' numerals reached Europe in the Middle Ages — partly through Spain — and slowly displaced Roman numerals.

From the sixteenth century the Mughal emperors ruled much of the north, patrons of painting, gardens and architecture. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal at Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631; its white marble seems to change colour with the hour. Later, the British East India Company extended its control, and after the rebellion of 1857 the British Crown ruled directly, in what became known as the Raj.

After a long struggle led by figures such as Mahatma Gandhi, whose campaigns of nonviolent civil disobedience inspired movements around the world, India became independent on 15 August 1947. Independence came with Partition, the division into India and Pakistan, which displaced over ten million people amid terrible violence. Today India is the most populous country on Earth and the world's largest democracy, where elections involve hundreds of millions of voters and take weeks to hold.

lb_egypt.title: Gift of the Nile: Ancient Egypt
lb_egypt.author: Dr. Amira Haddad
lb_egypt.desc: Pyramids, pharaohs and papyrus: an accessible history of ancient Egypt. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The Greek historian Herodotus called Egypt 'the gift of the Nile', and he was right. Each summer the river flooded, spreading black silt over the fields, and when the water withdrew the Egyptians planted in the richest soil in the Mediterranean world. They called their land Kemet, 'the black land', after that silt, and the desert beyond it Deshret, 'the red land'. Their calendar, their taxes and their gods all followed the rhythm of the flood.

The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BC. For about three thousand eight hundred years it remained the tallest structure made by human hands. It was not built by slaves, as once believed, but largely by paid and conscripted labourers, whose bakeries, breweries and cemeteries archaeologists have found nearby. Some of their work gangs scrawled cheerful names on the stones, such as 'Friends of Khufu'.

Egyptian writing — hieroglyphs for monuments and faster scripts for everyday use — was forgotten after the end of antiquity. Then, in 1799, French soldiers found a stone near Rosetta inscribed with the same decree in hieroglyphs, a later Egyptian script called Demotic, and Greek. Working from it, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion announced in 1822 that he had cracked the code, and the pharaohs began to speak again.

Egypt's history is so long that its ancient people were themselves tourists of their own past. The pharaoh Hatshepsut ruled for about two decades in the fifteenth century BC and sent a famous expedition to the land of Punt; Ramesses II reigned for sixty-six years and put his name on half the monuments in the country. Cleopatra VII, the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic kingdom, died in 30 BC — which means she lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.

The Nile still defines Egypt, though its flood no longer comes. The Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, tamed the river, providing electricity and year-round irrigation, but it also trapped the silt that once renewed the fields. Temples threatened by the rising waters behind the dam, including Abu Simbel, were cut into blocks and moved to higher ground in an international rescue effort. Ancient Egypt, it turns out, is still being carefully moved from place to place.

lb_rome.title: SPQR and the Rest of Us: A History of Rome
lb_rome.author: Marc Valls Tarradellas
lb_rome.desc: The rise and fall of Rome, written with a soft spot for Barcino. Library copy; do not remove.
text: According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC by Romulus, who promptly killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city walls. The Romans themselves enjoyed this story rather too much. By 509 BC they had expelled their last king and established a Republic ruled by elected magistrates and a Senate, and they came to loathe the very word 'king'. 'SPQR' — the Senate and the People of Rome — was stamped on everything from coins to drain covers, and still is, in modern Rome.

The Republic conquered Italy, then Carthage, then Greece and much of the Mediterranean, and in the process it strained and cracked. Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon with his army in 49 BC, won a civil war and was stabbed to death by senators on the Ides of March, 44 BC. His adopted heir Octavian defeated his rivals and in 27 BC accepted the name Augustus, becoming, in all but name, the first emperor. It was Augustus's colonists who laid out the little walled town of Barcino, which would become Barcelona.

Rome's genius was often practical. Its engineers built roads that ran straight for hundreds of kilometres, aqueducts that carried water across valleys, and a hydraulic concrete made with volcanic ash that set even under the sea. The dome of the Pantheon, completed under the emperor Hadrian around 125, is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. They also gave Europe its calendar, much of its law, and the Latin from which Catalan, Spanish, Italian, French, Portuguese and Romanian descend.

The empire grew too large to govern from one place and was eventually divided. In the West, under pressure from invading peoples and its own internal crises, the last emperor, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, was deposed in 476. The Eastern Empire, ruled from Constantinople, survived for nearly another thousand years, until the city fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Its citizens called themselves Romans to the very end.

Walk down Carrer del Paradís in the Gothic Quarter and you can still touch Rome: the four columns of the Temple of Augustus, and stretches of the old wall built into medieval houses. The city's Roman street plan survives in the lanes around the cathedral. Every time a Barcelonan says 'aigua' for water or 'pa' for bread, they are speaking a descendant of the Latin those colonists brought with them. Rome did not really fall. It simply changed its accent.

lb_vikings.title: Longships and Law-Speakers: The Viking Age
lb_vikings.author: Ingrid Solheim Puig
lb_vikings.desc: Raiders, traders and poets of the North. Contains no horned helmets whatsoever. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The Viking Age is conventionally dated from 793, when raiders from Scandinavia attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the coast of Northumbria. A shocked scholar at Charlemagne's court wrote that such a terror had never been seen in Britain. For the next two and a half centuries, Norse ships appeared along the coasts and rivers of Europe with alarming regularity. 'Viking' was originally something you went — raiding, 'a-viking' — rather than something you were.

Their secret was the longship: long, light, flexible, with a shallow draught that let it cross open sea and then row far up rivers. The Norse reached Iceland, Greenland and, around the year 1000, North America, where Leif Erikson's people built a settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, nearly five centuries before Columbus. Heading east, Swedish Norse travelled down the rivers of Russia to Constantinople, where the emperors recruited them into an elite bodyguard, the Varangian Guard.

They reached Iberia too. In 844 a Viking fleet sailed up the Guadalquivir and sacked Seville, before being defeated by the forces of the emir of Córdoba. Later raids struck along the coasts of the Mediterranean. In France, a Norse chieftain called Rollo was granted land in 911 in return for defending it against other raiders; his people became the Normans, and his descendant William conquered England in 1066.

Vikings were also farmers, merchants and lawmakers. In Iceland, free men gathered from 930 at the Althing, an open-air assembly where a Law-Speaker recited the laws from memory; it is often called the oldest surviving parliament in the world. They told their history in sagas and left inscriptions in runes. And they left their gods in our calendars: Wednesday is Woden's day, Thursday is Thor's day, and Friday belongs to Frigg.

As for the horned helmets: there is no evidence Vikings wore them in battle. The image owes much to nineteenth-century artists and, especially, to the costume designs for the first complete staging of Wagner's Ring cycle in 1876. A horned helmet would, after all, give an enemy two convenient handles. The real Vikings were more practical than that, which is why they got so far.

lb_mexico.title: The Eagle on the Cactus: A History of Mexico
lb_mexico.author: Ximena Robles i Prat
lb_mexico.desc: From maize to murals: a vivid history of Mexico. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Around nine thousand years ago, farmers in the south of what is now Mexico began domesticating a scrubby wild grass called teosinte. Over thousands of years of patient selection, it became maize — corn — one of the most important crops on Earth. Mexico also gave the world tomatoes, chillies, avocados and cacao, which means that much of what we now think of as Mediterranean cooking would be unrecognisable without it. Try to imagine pa amb tomàquet without the tomato.

The Olmecs, from around 1200 BC, carved colossal stone heads, some nearly three metres tall, and are often called the 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica. The Maya developed a sophisticated writing system, astronomy and a calendar of interlocking cycles, and built cities of pyramids in the rainforest. Teotihuacan, near modern Mexico City, was at its height one of the largest cities in the world, with an avenue so grand that the later Aztecs, finding it in ruins, called it the Avenue of the Dead.

The Mexica, or Aztecs, founded their capital Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco, where, according to legend, they saw an eagle perched on a cactus — the image on Mexico's flag today.
