It grew into a city of causeways, canals and floating gardens that astonished the Spanish when they arrived. In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast; by 1521, with the help of indigenous allies and devastated by smallpox, the city had fallen. Mexico City was built on its ruins, and it is still slowly sinking into the old lake bed.

For three centuries the region was the Viceroyalty of New Spain. On 16 September 1810 the priest Miguel Hidalgo rang the church bell in the town of Dolores and called for revolt — the 'Grito de Dolores', still re-enacted every year by the president. Independence came in 1821. A century later, the Mexican Revolution of 1910 overthrew a long dictatorship and reshaped the country through a decade of war.

The Revolution produced the great muralists — Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros — who painted Mexico's history across the walls of public buildings, so that anyone could read it. Rivera's wife, Frida Kahlo, painted smaller, fiercer self-portraits that have since become known all over the world. Mexico today is home to more Spanish speakers than any other country, and to dozens of living indigenous languages as well.

lb_brazil.title: A Country Named After a Tree: A History of Brazil
lb_brazil.author: Rafael Teixeira Soler
lb_brazil.desc: Sugar, gold, samba and a capital built from scratch. Library copy; do not remove.
text: In 1494, two years after Columbus's first voyage, Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a line down the Atlantic and dividing the newly known world between them. The line happened to leave the eastern bulge of South America on the Portuguese side. In 1500 the navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral, sailing for India, swung wide into the Atlantic and landed there, claiming the land for Portugal. The indigenous peoples who had lived there for thousands of years were not consulted.

The land took its name from a tree. Brazilwood, pau-brasil, yielded a precious red dye — 'brasa' means ember — and the coast became known as the land of brazilwood, then simply Brazil. Sugar plantations followed, then a gold rush in Minas Gerais in the eighteenth century. All of it was built on the forced labour of enslaved Africans; Brazil received more enslaved people than any other country in the Americas, and it was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, with the Golden Law of 1888.

In 1808, fleeing Napoleon's invasion of Portugal, the entire Portuguese royal court sailed to Rio de Janeiro, making it the only European colonial capital ever to host its own monarchy. When the king returned to Lisbon, his son Pedro stayed behind and in 1822 declared Brazil independent, becoming its emperor. The monarchy lasted until 1889, when a military coup proclaimed a republic.

In 1960 Brazil inaugurated a new capital in the interior, Brasília, built almost from nothing in about four years. The urban planner Lúcio Costa laid it out in the shape of an aeroplane — or a bird, depending on whom you ask — and the architect Oscar Niemeyer filled it with sweeping white modernist buildings. It was meant to pull the country's development inland, away from the crowded coast.

Brazil is the largest country in South America and the largest Portuguese-speaking nation in the world. Much of the Amazon rainforest, which plays a vital role in the planet's climate, lies within its borders. It has given the world samba, bossa nova and the idea that football can be played as though it were a dance. It is also, pleasingly, the only country whose name comes from a piece of firewood.

lb_germany.title: The Restless Middle: A History of Germany
lb_germany.author: Katrin Albrecht
lb_germany.desc: A sober, humane history of the lands at the heart of Europe. Library copy; do not remove.
text: For most of its history, Germany was not a country but a patchwork: hundreds of duchies, bishoprics, free cities and principalities loosely gathered under the Holy Roman Empire, which Voltaire famously mocked as neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. That patchwork gave Germany its many dialects, its regional pride and its habit of having a respectable opera house in almost every mid-sized town. It also made unity, when it came, a late and complicated affair.

Around 1450, in Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable metal type, and a revolution in knowledge followed. In 1517 a monk named Martin Luther published his Ninety-Five Theses criticising the sale of indulgences, and thanks to the printing press his ideas spread faster than anyone could suppress them. His translation of the Bible helped shape the modern German language. The religious wars that followed culminated in the Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648, which devastated the German lands.

Germany was unified under Prussian leadership in 1871, with Otto von Bismarck as its chancellor, and rapidly became an industrial and scientific powerhouse. Defeat in the First World War brought the fragile Weimar Republic, and economic catastrophe helped bring the Nazis to power in 1933. Their dictatorship led the world into the Second World War and carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of six million Jews and of millions of others. Germany's reckoning with this history, known as Vergangenheitsbewältigung, remains central to its identity.

After 1945 the country was divided: the Federal Republic in the west, a founding member of what became the European Union, and the German Democratic Republic in the east, within the Soviet bloc. In 1961 the East built the Berlin Wall to stop its citizens leaving. On 9 November 1989, amid peaceful mass protests, the Wall was opened, and on 3 October 1990 Germany was reunified. That day is now a national holiday.

Modern Germany is a federal republic of sixteen states, proud of its constitution, its bread and its trains, though the trains are a sensitive subject. It is the European Union's most populous member and largest economy, and a keen participant in Erasmus: tens of thousands of German students go abroad each year. Many of them, it is said, come home with a new appreciation for late dinners and a lasting inability to tolerate bad coffee.

lb_italy.title: A Boot Full of Cities: A History of Italy
lb_italy.author: Giulia Ferraro Mas
lb_italy.desc: From city-states to a republic, with frequent pauses for lunch. Library copy; do not remove.
text: After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Italian peninsula spent more than a thousand years divided. Powerful city-states — Venice, Genoa, Florence, Milan — grew rich on trade and banking, while the Papal States held the centre and foreign powers fought over the south. Venice, built on wooden piles driven into a lagoon, ruled a maritime empire for centuries and was known simply as La Serenissima, the Most Serene. Catalan merchants knew these rivals well, and fought Genoa at sea more than once.

Italian as a written language owes an enormous debt to Dante Alighieri, whose Divine Comedy, completed shortly before his death in 1321, was written not in Latin but in the Tuscan vernacular of Florence. Petrarch and Boccaccio followed, and Tuscan became the basis of the literary language. When Italy finally unified, only a small fraction of its people actually spoke that standard Italian at home; the rest spoke regional languages that are still alive today.

In fifteenth-century Florence, bankers like the Medici paid for an explosion of art and learning that we call the Renaissance. Brunelleschi raised the great dome of Florence Cathedral without a full supporting frame; Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks with flying machines and anatomy; Michelangelo carved the David from a block of marble other sculptors had given up on. The idea that one person could be an artist, engineer and scientist all at once owes much to this moment.

Unification, the Risorgimento, came in stages. In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi landed in Sicily with his 'Thousand' volunteers in red shirts and conquered the south; in 1861 the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed; in 1871 Rome became its capital. The politician Massimo d'Azeglio is credited with the remark that, having made Italy, they now had to make Italians — a task some would say is still pleasantly unfinished.

After the Fascist dictatorship of Mussolini and the Second World War, Italians voted in a referendum in 1946 to abolish the monarchy and become a republic. In 1957 Italy was one of the six founders of the European Economic Community, and the treaty was signed in Rome. It gave the world opera, the university — Bologna's, founded in 1088, is often called the oldest in continuous operation — and an unshakeable conviction that cappuccino is not to be drunk after eleven in the morning.

lb_england.title: Rain, Rights and Revolutions: A History of England
lb_england.author: Oliver Pemberton-Soler
lb_england.desc: An affectionate history of England from 1066 to the Industrial Revolution. Library copy; do not remove.
text: In 1066 Duke William of Normandy crossed the Channel, defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings, and became William the Conqueror. The Normans built castles, compiled the Domesday Book — an astonishingly detailed survey of land and livestock — and brought French into the court. English survived among ordinary people, soaking up thousands of French words; this is why English has 'cow' in the field and 'beef' on the plate, 'pig' in the sty and 'pork' at dinner.

In 1215, rebellious barons forced King John to agree to a charter at Runnymede, beside the Thames. Magna Carta was largely a list of specific grievances, and it was annulled within weeks, but it established a powerful principle: that the king himself was subject to the law. Reissued and reinterpreted over centuries, it became a symbol of liberty far beyond England, and it influenced constitutions on the other side of the world.

The Tudors gave England Henry VIII, who broke with Rome in the 1530s so that he could end his marriage, and his daughter Elizabeth I, under whom English drama flourished with Marlowe and Shakespeare. In 1588 Philip II of Spain sent a great Armada to invade England; it was defeated in the Channel and then scattered by storms around Scotland and Ireland. The Spanish and the English still disagree about exactly how much credit the weather deserves.

In the seventeenth century, conflict between Crown and Parliament led to civil war, and in 1649 King Charles I was tried and beheaded. After a brief republic under Oliver Cromwell, the monarchy returned, and in 1688 the 'Glorious Revolution' replaced James II with William and Mary and established the supremacy of Parliament. In 1707 the Acts of Union joined England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain.

From the late eighteenth century, the Industrial Revolution began in the mills and mines of northern England. Steam engines, spinning machines and railways transformed how people worked and lived, crowding them into fast-growing cities and producing both vast wealth and terrible poverty — the very conditions Cerdà studied in Barcelona. England also gave the world football, which Barcelona has since, many would argue, perfected.

lb_sweden.title: Light in the North: A History of Sweden
lb_sweden.author: Astrid Lindqvist Roca
lb_sweden.desc: Kings, a sinking warship and the right to roam. Library copy; do not remove.
text: In 1523 a nobleman named Gustav Vasa, having led a rebellion against the Danish king who ruled the Kalmar Union, was elected King of Sweden. His date of election, 6 June, is now Sweden's national day. Gustav built a strong central state and broke with the Catholic Church, and his dynasty would lead Sweden to the height of its power. Every year thousands of skiers race ninety kilometres in the Vasaloppet, retracing a legendary flight of the young Gustav.

In the seventeenth century, under Gustavus Adolphus, Sweden became a great European power, winning battles in the Thirty Years' War and controlling much of the Baltic coast. Ambition sometimes outran engineering. In 1628 the magnificent warship Vasa, built to be the pride of the navy, sailed out of Stockholm harbour on her maiden voyage, heeled over in a light breeze and sank after little more than a kilometre. Raised almost intact in 1961, she is now the most visited museum in Scandinavia, and a permanent lesson in the dangers of adding one more row of cannons.

Sweden's great-power era ended with defeat by Russia in the early eighteenth century. Its last war was fought in 1814, and for the following two centuries the country followed a policy of neutrality, staying out of both world wars. That long peace allowed Sweden to develop into one of the most prosperous and egalitarian societies in the world. In 2024, in response to a changed security situation, it joined NATO.

Sweden has given the world some useful words. The 'ombudsman', an official who investigates citizens' complaints against the government, was established in Sweden in 1809 and has been copied across the globe. The chemist Alfred Nobel, inventor of dynamite, left most of his fortune to fund prizes 'to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind'; the first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901.

Swedes also enjoy allemansrätten, the 'right of public access', which allows anyone to walk, camp for a night and pick berries and mushrooms on most land, as long as they do not disturb or destroy. It is summed up in the phrase 'don't disturb, don't destroy'. Long winters have made Swedes connoisseurs of candles and coffee breaks — the fika — and of the long light of midsummer, which they celebrate by dancing around a maypole like frogs.

lb_silkroad.title: Threads Across the World: The Silk Roads
lb_silkroad.author: Farid Nazari & Laia Grau
lb_silkroad.desc: Silk, paper, faith and plague on the great trade routes of Asia. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The name 'Silk Road' is surprisingly recent. It was coined in 1877 by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen, and it describes something that was never a single road. It was a shifting web of routes, over mountains and deserts and by sea, linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia, Arabia and the Mediterranean. Most goods travelled only part of the way, changing hands many times in oasis cities before reaching their final buyers.

The traffic began in earnest in the second century BC, when the Han emperor sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, westward to find allies against the nomadic Xiongnu. He was captured and held for ten years, escaped, and returned with reports of rich kingdoms and remarkable horses. China began to trade silk for those horses, and the Romans, a world away, developed an expensive taste for silk so fine that moralists complained it made clothing indecently transparent.

Much more than silk travelled. Paper spread westward from China to the Islamic world, and from there, via al-Andalus, into Europe. Buddhism journeyed from India into China along the routes, leaving painted caves at Dunhuang. Spices, glass, horses, music, mathematics and medicine were exchanged, and so were diseases: the Black Death, which killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population in the 1340s, almost certainly travelled west along these trading networks.

Oasis cities grew fabulously rich on the traffic. Samarkand, in today's Uzbekistan, became famous for its blue-tiled mosques and madrasas. In the thirteenth century, when the Mongol Empire controlled much of the route, travel became unusually safe, and a Venetian merchant's son named Marco Polo made his famous journey to the court of Kublai Khan, returning after twenty-four years with stories many people refused to believe.

The rise of sea routes and the break-up of the Mongol Empire gradually reduced the overland trade. But the Silk Roads had already stitched the Old World together, and in 2014 UNESCO inscribed a five-thousand-kilometre section of routes through China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan as a World Heritage site. Every time you write on paper or count with zero, you are using something that probably travelled those roads.

lb_coldwar.title: The Long Standoff: The Cold War, 1947–1991
lb_coldwar.author: Dr. Tomasz Nowak Pujol
lb_coldwar.desc: A clear-eyed account of the four-decade stand-off between East and West. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The Cold War was called cold because the two superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union, never fought each other directly. Instead they competed through alliances, arms races, propaganda, espionage, space programmes and wars fought by others. It began in the years after 1945, as wartime allies divided a ruined Europe between them, and Winston Churchill spoke in 1946 of an 'iron curtain' descending across the continent from the Baltic to the Adriatic.

In 1947 the Truman Doctrine pledged American support for countries resisting communism, and the Marshall Plan poured aid into Western Europe's recovery. In 1948 the Soviets blockaded West Berlin; for almost a year the Western allies supplied the city entirely by air, landing a plane every few minutes at the height of the airlift. NATO was founded in 1949, and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. Germany, and Berlin itself, were split down the middle.

The closest the world came to nuclear war was probably October 1962, when American reconnaissance photographs revealed Soviet missiles being installed in Cuba. For thirteen days, the two sides stood at the brink, until Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles and the United States secretly agreed to withdraw its own from Turkey. The fright led, in 1963, to a direct 'hotline' between Washington and Moscow, so that the leaders could talk before anyone did something irreversible.

The conflict had many faces: the Korean and Vietnam wars, coups and revolutions across Latin America, Africa and Asia, the space race, chess matches and Olympic boycotts. Periods of tension alternated with détente and arms-control treaties. Behind the Iron Curtain, uprisings in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 were crushed, but dissent never disappeared, and in Poland the Solidarity trade union grew into a mass movement in the 1980s.

In 1985 Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader and began reforms — glasnost, openness, and perestroika, restructuring — that he could not control. In 1989 the communist regimes of Eastern Europe fell one after another, mostly peacefully, and on 9 November crowds began to tear down the Berlin Wall. On 26 December 1991 the Soviet Union formally dissolved. The world that followed has been complicated in its own ways, but a generation was spared the war that everyone had feared.

lb_democracy.title: Rule by the Many: A History of Democracy
lb_democracy.author: Helena Stavrou i Riera
lb_democracy.desc: From Athenian pebbles to universal suffrage, and why it keeps having to be reinvented. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The word democracy comes from the Greek dēmos, the people, and kratos, power. In 508 or 507 BC the Athenian statesman Cleisthenes reorganised the city so that power rested with an assembly of citizens, who met on a hillside called the Pnyx to debate and vote on laws, war and peace. Many public offices were filled not by election but by lot, on the grounds that elections favour the rich and the well known. It was a radical idea, and it worked, on and off, for nearly two centuries.

Athenian democracy had severe limits. Citizenship was restricted to adult men of Athenian parentage; women, slaves and foreign residents — the majority of the population — had no vote. Citizens could also 'ostracise' a powerful politician: each wrote a name on a shard of pottery, an ostrakon, and if enough votes were cast, the person with the most had to leave the city for ten years. It was a peaceful way of getting rid of someone who seemed to be growing too dangerous.

Elsewhere, assemblies and councils developed in many forms. In 930 the Icelanders founded the Althing, often called the oldest surviving parliament. In 1215 Magna Carta asserted that even a king was bound by law, and in the thirteenth century the Catalan Corts and the English Parliament both began to meet regularly. None of these was a democracy in the modern sense, but each helped establish the principle that rulers need the consent of the ruled.

The modern revival began with revolutions in America and France in the late eighteenth century, which proclaimed that sovereignty belonged to the people. The American Constitution of 1787 created an elected government with separated powers. Yet for a long time 'the people' meant only some men. New Zealand became the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections in 1893. Switzerland, one of the world's oldest democracies, only granted women the vote at federal level in 1971.

Democracy is not only voting. It depends on free speech, a free press, independent courts, the protection of minorities and the peaceful handing-over of power to the winner of an election, however disappointing. Winston Churchill told the House of Commons in 1947 that democracy was the worst form of government except all those other forms that had been tried. It has to be relearned by every generation — which is, perhaps, why it is taught in libraries.

lb_revolutions.title: The World Turned Upside Down: Revolutions
lb_revolutions.author: Dr. Àngel Bosch
lb_revolutions.desc: Barricades, manifestos and unintended consequences, from 1776 to 1989. Library copy; do not remove.
text: A revolution is more than a change of government. It is a sudden, often violent transformation of who holds power and why — and it very rarely turns out the way its first leaders intended. In 1776 thirteen British colonies in North America declared their independence, asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with rights to 'life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness'. The men who signed those words included slaveholders, a contradiction that would haunt the new republic for generations.

On 14 July 1789 the people of Paris stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, which at that moment held just seven prisoners. It was a symbolic act, and symbols matter in revolutions: the day is now France's national holiday. The French Revolution abolished feudal privileges, declared the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, executed a king, spread its ideals by war across Europe — and passed through the Terror before ending in the dictatorship of Napoleon.

The most radical revolution of the age took place in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. In 1791 enslaved people rose up against their masters, and after years of war, led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture, they defeated the armies of France, Spain and Britain. In 1804 Haiti declared its independence: the first nation born of a successful slave revolt. It was forced for over a century to pay crushing reparations to France for its own freedom.

In 1848 revolutions broke out across Europe, from Paris to Vienna and Berlin — the 'Springtime of Nations'. Most were suppressed within a year, but they left behind new constitutions, the end of serfdom in parts of central Europe, and ideas that would not go away. In 1917 revolution in Russia overthrew the Tsar and then, in the October Revolution — which took place in November by our calendar — brought the Bolsheviks to power, with consequences that shaped the whole twentieth century.

Some revolutions have been gentle. On 25 April 1974, a largely bloodless military coup in Portugal ended decades of dictatorship; soldiers wore red carnations in their rifle barrels, and it became the Carnation Revolution. In 1989 Czechoslovakia's communist regime fell after weeks of peaceful mass protest in the Velvet Revolution, led in part by the playwright Václav Havel. A revolution, it turns out, can be won with flowers and keys — protesters in Prague jingled their keys to say goodbye.

lb_transition.title: From Dictatorship to Democracy: Spain's Transition, 1975–1982
lb_transition.author: Dr. Elena Martí Ruiz
lb_transition.desc: A careful, balanced account of how Spain became a democracy, and the debates that continue. Library copy; do not remove.
text: General Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975, after ruling Spain since his victory in the Civil War of 1936–1939. Two days later Juan Carlos de Borbón, whom Franco had chosen as his successor, was proclaimed king. Many expected the dictatorship's institutions to continue with little change. Instead, over the following years, Spain moved from dictatorship to parliamentary democracy through a negotiated process that historians call the Transition, la Transición.

In 1976 the king appointed Adolfo Suárez, a relatively young official from within the old regime, as prime minister. Suárez steered the Law for Political Reform through the Francoist parliament — which effectively voted to dissolve itself — and it was approved by a referendum in December 1976. Political parties, including the Communist Party in April 1977, were legalised. On 15 June 1977, Spaniards voted in their first free general election in over forty years, and Suárez's centrist coalition won.

Much of the Transition rested on negotiation between former adversaries. The Moncloa Pacts of 1977 brought government, opposition parties and unions together to tackle inflation and economic crisis. An Amnesty Law in the same year freed political prisoners, but it also shielded officials of the dictatorship from prosecution for past crimes. The Constitution, drafted by representatives of the main parties, was approved by referendum on 6 December 1978, establishing a parliamentary monarchy and recognising the right to autonomy of Spain's nationalities and regions.

In Catalonia, the Generalitat — the historic Catalan government — was provisionally restored in 1977, and its president in exile, Josep Tarradellas, returned to Barcelona, greeting the crowd from the balcony with the words 'Ciutadans de Catalunya, ja sóc aquí!' — 'Citizens of Catalonia, I am here at last!' A Statute of Autonomy followed in 1979. On 23 February 1981 a group of Civil Guards led by Antonio Tejero stormed the Congress during a vote, but the coup attempt collapsed within hours after the king publicly backed the constitution. In 1982 the Socialist Party won a large majority, and power passed peacefully to the former opposition.

Historians and citizens continue to debate the Transition. Many regard it as a model of peaceful democratisation, achieved through compromise in difficult circumstances, and point to decades of stable democracy and Spain's entry into the European Community in 1986. Others argue that the price of consensus was a 'pact of forgetting', which left victims of the Civil War and the dictatorship without justice or recognition, and that many unresolved questions were postponed rather than settled. Laws on historical memory in 2007 and 2022 have sought to address some of these issues, and the debate itself is part of the democracy the Transition built.

lb_un.title: We the Peoples: The United Nations
lb_un.author: Amara Okafor Casals
lb_un.desc: How the world tried to organise its peace after 1945. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 by fifty countries, with Poland signing soon after as the fifty-first original member, and it came into force on 24 October 1945 — now celebrated as United Nations Day. Its opening words, 'We the peoples of the United Nations, determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war', were written in the shadow of the deadliest conflict in history. Its predecessor, the League of Nations, had failed to prevent that war.

The General Assembly gives every member state one vote, from the largest to the smallest; today there are 193 members. The Security Council is different: five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — each hold a veto over its decisions, alongside ten members elected for two-year terms. The veto was the price of bringing the great powers inside the organisation, and it remains its most controversial feature.

On 10 December 1948 the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, drafted by a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt. It was not a binding treaty, but it set out, for the first time, rights belonging to every human being, and it has been translated into more languages than almost any other document. Its first article begins: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'

UN peacekeepers, wearing their distinctive blue helmets, have served in dozens of missions around the world since 1948, and in 1988 the peacekeeping forces received the Nobel Peace Prize. The UN family also includes agencies such as UNICEF for children, the World Health Organization, and UNESCO, which lists World Heritage Sites — including several in Barcelona by Gaudí and by Domènech i Montaner.

Spain joined the United Nations in 1955. Critics of the UN point to deadlocked councils and conflicts it failed to prevent; its defenders reply that it was never meant to take us to heaven, but to save us from hell — a line usually attributed to its second Secretary-General, Dag Hammarskjöld. Both views contain truth. It remains the only place where nearly every country on Earth sits in the same room.

lb_greekphil.title: Questions in the Agora: Greek Philosophy
lb_greekphil.author: Dr. Nikos Papadakis i Serra
lb_greekphil.desc: From Thales to the Stoics: how the Greeks learned to argue about everything. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Western philosophy is conventionally said to begin with Thales of Miletus, in the sixth century BC, who proposed that everything is ultimately made of water. He was wrong, but gloriously so: he was trying to explain the world by reason rather than myth. Anaximander suggested the boundless, Anaximenes air, and Heraclitus argued that everything is in flux, observing that you cannot step into the same river twice, because other waters are always flowing on. Parmenides replied that change is an illusion, and the argument has never really stopped.

Socrates wrote nothing. He wandered the agora of Athens asking people what they meant by justice, courage or piety, and demonstrating, patiently and sometimes infuriatingly, that they did not know. He claimed his only wisdom was knowing that he knew nothing. In 399 BC the Athenians tried him for impiety and corrupting the young, and he was sentenced to die by drinking hemlock. He could have escaped; he chose to obey the laws of his city.

His student Plato wrote dialogues starring Socrates and founded the Academy around 387 BC, one of the first institutions of higher learning in the West. Plato argued that the things we see are imperfect copies of eternal Forms, and in his allegory of the cave he pictured humanity as prisoners mistaking shadows on a wall for reality. Every student who has ever sat in a dark lecture hall, watching slides, has found this uncomfortably apt.

Plato's student Aristotle wrote on almost everything: logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, poetry. He was tutor to the young Alexander the Great and founded his own school, the Lyceum. Where Plato looked upward to ideal Forms, Aristotle looked closely at the world around him, dissecting animals and classifying constitutions. His idea that virtue is a mean between extremes — courage lies between cowardice and recklessness — remains remarkably practical advice.

Later schools asked how to live well. The Epicureans sought a calm, pleasant life among friends, in a garden, free from fear of the gods and of death. The Stoics, named after the painted porch, the Stoa, where Zeno of Citium taught, urged people to accept what they cannot control and master what they can: their own judgements. And Diogenes the Cynic lived in a large storage jar; when Alexander the Great offered him anything he wished, he is said to have asked him to step aside, as he was blocking the sun.

lb_money.title: Shells, Coins and Code: A History of Money
lb_money.author: Dr. Gabriel Ferrer Lindahl
lb_money.desc: What money is, where it came from, and why a piece of paper buys a croissant. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Economics textbooks long taught that money was invented to replace barter: a farmer with wheat who wanted shoes had to find a shoemaker who wanted wheat, which was inconvenient, so money was invented. Anthropologists have spent a century looking for societies that actually ran on barter and have found remarkably few. Instead, early economies often ran on credit and obligation — I give you grain now, you owe me — recorded in memory or, in Mesopotamia, on clay tablets thousands of years ago.

The first coins appeared in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, around the late seventh century BC, made of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, and stamped to guarantee their weight. The idea spread rapidly through the Greek world and beyond. Money has also taken many other forms: cowrie shells, salt, cattle, and on the island of Yap in the Pacific, enormous stone discs called rai, some too heavy to move, whose ownership changed hands while the stone itself stayed exactly where it was.

Paper money appeared in China. Merchants in Sichuan began using paper certificates in the Song dynasty, and in the early eleventh century the government took over their issue, creating what is usually regarded as the first government-backed paper currency. When Marco Polo described paper money in the thirteenth century, Europeans found it one of the least believable parts of his story. They would get used to it.

For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, major currencies were tied to gold: in principle, you could exchange notes for a fixed amount of metal. The system was strained by war and depression, and in 1971 President Nixon ended the direct convertibility of the US dollar into gold. Since then the major currencies have been 'fiat' money: valuable not because of what they are made of, but because governments accept them for taxes and because we all trust that others will accept them tomorrow.

On 1 January 2002 euro notes and coins entered circulation in twelve countries, including Spain and Germany. Each euro coin has a common side and a national side; Spain's one- and two-euro coins bear the portrait of the King. Today, most money exists only as numbers in bank computers, and tapping a card to buy a croissant sets off a small cascade of digital promises. Money, in the end, is a story we tell each other, and so far, mostly, we keep believing it.

lb_trade.title: Ships, Silk and Spreadsheets: A History of Trade
lb_trade.author: Jordi Llobet Andersson
lb_trade.desc: Why people swap things, from the Hanseatic League to the shipping container. Library copy; do not remove.
text: People have traded across great distances for as long as there have been people. Obsidian, a volcanic glass prized for its razor edge, was carried hundreds of kilometres in the Stone Age; amber from the Baltic reached the Mediterranean; tin from Cornwall helped make the bronze of the eastern Mediterranean. Trade spread goods, but also techniques, words, recipes, gods and genes. A good part of history is simply the story of who bought what from whom.

In the Middle Ages, Barcelona was one of the great trading cities of the Mediterranean, and its merchants helped write the rules of the sea. The Llibre del Consolat de Mar, a compilation of Catalan maritime customs and law from the fourteenth century, governed disputes over cargo, shipwreck and contracts and was used in ports across the Mediterranean for centuries. In the north, the Hanseatic League, an alliance of merchant towns such as Lübeck and Hamburg, dominated Baltic and North Sea trade.

In 1817 the English economist David Ricardo explained why trade benefits both sides even when one is better at everything. His example was England and Portugal, cloth and wine. Even if Portugal could produce both more efficiently, both countries would gain if each specialised in what it produced at the lowest opportunity cost — what it gave up least to make — and traded. This principle, comparative advantage, remains one of the most important and least intuitive ideas in economics.

In 1956 an American trucking businessman, Malcom McLean, sent a converted tanker from New Jersey to Texas carrying fifty-eight metal boxes that could be lifted straight from truck to ship. The standard shipping container slashed the cost of loading and unloading and transformed global trade; nearly everything you own has probably spent some time inside one. Walk past the Port of Barcelona and you will see them stacked like enormous coloured bricks.

After the Second World War, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed in 1947, gradually lowered barriers between countries, and in 1995 it was succeeded by the World Trade Organization. Trade has lifted many countries out of poverty, while also bringing painful change to workers and regions whose industries moved elsewhere. Economists broadly agree about the gains; the harder question, as always, is how to share them.

lb_keynes.title: Keynes vs Hayek: The Great Debate
lb_keynes.author: Dr. Ricard Pons & Dr. Anna Weiss
lb_keynes.desc: The two economists whose argument shaped the twentieth century, presented fairly to both. Library copy; do not remove.
text: In the early 1930s, as the Great Depression threw millions out of work, two brilliant economists offered opposite diagnoses. John Maynard Keynes, a Cambridge don, patron of the arts and speculator, argued that economies could get stuck with high unemployment for long periods because there was not enough total spending. Friedrich Hayek, a young Austrian at the London School of Economics, argued that the slump was the painful correction of an earlier boom fuelled by cheap credit, and that government meddling would only make things worse.

Keynes set out his ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936. When households and businesses cut back spending out of fear, he argued, one person's cut becomes another's lost income, and the whole economy can spiral downward. In such conditions, governments should step in, spending and borrowing to support demand until confidence returns. 'In the long run', he famously remarked of economists who counselled patience, 'we are all dead.'

Hayek, in The Road to Serfdom of 1944, warned that extensive central planning, however well-intentioned, risks eroding individual freedom, because planners cannot possess the knowledge scattered among millions of people. Prices, he argued, are a marvellous information system, signalling what is scarce and what is wanted without anyone needing to understand the whole picture. Distort them, and you blind the economy.

The two men disagreed fiercely in print, but they were personally cordial. During the Second World War, when the LSE was evacuated to Cambridge, Keynes helped find Hayek rooms, and the story goes that the two took turns fire-watching for German bombs on the roof of King's College Chapel. Keynes died in 1946, his ideas dominant for the next three decades. Hayek lived long enough to see his own come back into fashion, and shared the Nobel Prize in economics in 1974.

Today, most economists draw on both. Keynes's insights shaped the response to the global financial crisis of 2008 and to the pandemic slump of 2020; Hayek's warnings about knowledge, prices and the limits of planning remain powerful. In 2010 two economists even made a rap video, 'Fear the Boom and Bust', staging the debate as a hip-hop battle. The argument continues, which is exactly how economics is supposed to work.

lb_smith.title: The Absent-Minded Professor: Adam Smith
lb_smith.author: Dr. Fiona MacLeod i Pla
lb_smith.desc: The life and ideas of the father of economics, who was far more than 'the invisible hand'. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Adam Smith was born in 1723 in Kirkcaldy, a small port on the Firth of Forth in Scotland, and was famously absent-minded: stories tell of him walking for miles in his dressing gown lost in thought, and of him once, deep in conversation, stepping straight into a tanning pit. He studied at Glasgow and Oxford, where he found the teaching lazy, and became a professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow. His first great book was not about economics at all.

The Theory of Moral Sentiments, published in 1759, asked how people come to judge right and wrong. Smith argued that we imagine how others see us, and consult an 'impartial spectator' within ourselves. Human beings, he wrote, are shaped by sympathy — our capacity to feel with others. He regarded it as his better book, and anyone who thinks Smith believed that selfishness is the whole of human nature should begin here.

In 1776 he published An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations. It opens with a pin factory, where ten workers, each specialising in one step, could make tens of thousands of pins a day, while one worker alone could hardly make twenty. The division of labour, Smith argued, was the great source of rising productivity. He also wrote the line every economics student learns: 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.'

The phrase 'invisible hand', for which he is so often remembered, appears only once in The Wealth of Nations, and only a handful of times in all his writings. Smith was deeply suspicious of merchants who conspired to raise prices, and wrote that people of the same trade seldom meet together, even for merriment, without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public. He supported public education and argued that the rich should contribute to public expenses in proportion to their means.

Smith spent his last years in Edinburgh as a commissioner of customs — a curious job for the great advocate of free trade — and died there in 1790, having ordered most of his unpublished papers burned. His portrait appeared on the Bank of England's twenty-pound note. He would probably have been embarrassed by the fuss, and then asked the price of the paper.

lb_maps.title: Drawing the World: A History of Maps
lb_maps.author: Cresques Vidal Abrams
lb_maps.desc: From clay tablets to the Catalan Atlas to GPS. Library copy; do not remove.
text: The oldest surviving map of the world is a small Babylonian clay tablet from around the sixth century BC. It shows Babylon near the centre, the Euphrates running through it, all surrounded by a ring of ocean with mysterious triangular regions beyond. It is not accurate, and it was not meant to be; like many maps, it is as much a picture of how people understood their place in the universe as of where things actually were.

In the second century, the Greek scholar Claudius Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, wrote his Geography, listing the coordinates of thousands of places using latitude and longitude. His original maps were lost, but his method survived, and when his work was rediscovered in Renaissance Europe it transformed mapmaking. His errors survived too: he underestimated the size of the Earth, which helped convince Columbus that Asia lay just a short sail west of Spain.

The Catalan Atlas of 1375 is one of the most beautiful maps ever made. Attributed to Cresques Abraham, a Jewish cartographer of Mallorca, it covers the known world from the Atlantic to China in gold, silver and bright colours, with compass lines radiating across the sea. It shows Mansa Musa, the fabulously rich king of Mali, holding a golden nugget, and a camel caravan crossing the Silk Road. It was given to the King of France, and it is still in Paris.

In 1569 the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator published a world map on which any straight line was a line of constant compass bearing — perfect for sailors. The price was distortion: areas near the poles are hugely enlarged. On a Mercator map Greenland looks about the size of Africa, though Africa is in fact around fourteen times larger. Other projections try to show true areas; every flat map of a round world must choose what to get wrong.

Today, satellites and the Global Positioning System allow a phone to locate you to within a few metres, and digital maps redraw themselves as you walk. Yet we still use Ptolemy's latitude and longitude, and we still argue about projections. Every map, from a clay tablet to your phone, is an argument about what matters. The best way to understand a city is still to walk it, with a paper map folded wrongly in your pocket.

lb_oceans.title: The Blue Planet: A History of the Oceans
lb_oceans.author: Dr. Marina Costa Olsen
lb_oceans.desc: Depths, currents and the long human effort to understand the sea. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Oceans cover about seventy-one per cent of the Earth's surface and hold around ninety-seven per cent of its water. They are, on average, nearly four kilometres deep. It is often said that we have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own seafloor, and for detailed, high-resolution mapping this is still broadly true. Seen from space, our planet is not really Earth at all; it is Ocean, with some islands.

Modern oceanography began with the voyage of HMS Challenger from 1872 to 1876, which sailed nearly 130,000 kilometres, took soundings of the deep, collected thousands of new species and discovered the Mariana Trench. Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, lies nearly eleven kilometres below the surface — if Mount Everest were dropped into it, its summit would still be under more than two kilometres of water. In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom in the bathyscaphe Trieste.

The oceans shape the climate. Great currents such as the Gulf Stream carry warm water north, which is part of why western Europe is milder than places at the same latitude in Canada. The ocean has absorbed around a quarter of the carbon dioxide humans have emitted and the great majority of the extra heat, which has slowed warming on land but made the seas warmer and more acidic. Tiny marine plants, phytoplankton, produce a large share of the oxygen we breathe.

Down the middle of the Atlantic runs the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain range where the seafloor is slowly spreading apart, pushing the Americas away from Europe and Africa by a few centimetres a year — roughly the speed at which your fingernails grow. Along such ridges, hydrothermal vents pour out hot, mineral-rich water, and around them live communities of creatures that depend not on sunlight but on chemical energy.

The Mediterranean, by comparison, is small, warm, salty and almost tideless, and yet it teems with life: dolphins, turtles, bluefin tuna and, in spring, the meadows of Posidonia seagrass that keep the water off Barcelona's beaches clear. Oceans are enormous, but they are not infinite, and they are not immune to us. Stand on the beach and look out. Almost everything beyond the horizon is still waiting to be understood.

lb_space.title: Race to the Moon: The Space Age
lb_space.author: Dr. Pedro Alcalde Nilsson
lb_space.desc: Sputnik, Gagarin, Apollo and a handshake in orbit. Library copy; do not remove.
text: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a polished metal sphere about the size of a beach ball, which circled the Earth every ninety-six minutes, beeping. Anyone with a radio could hear it. The United States was shaken; if the Soviets could put a satellite in orbit, they could deliver a warhead. A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog, Laika, the first animal to orbit the Earth. She did not survive the flight, and her story still makes people sad.

On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting the Earth once in Vostok 1 in a flight lasting about 108 minutes. 'Poyekhali!' — 'Let's go!' — he said at lift-off. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, spending nearly three days in orbit. The Soviets seemed to be winning every lap of the race.

In 1961 President John F. Kennedy committed the United States to landing a man on the Moon before the decade was out. The Apollo programme employed some four hundred thousand people. On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the lunar module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquillity, while Michael Collins orbited overhead, and Armstrong stepped onto the surface. Around six hundred million people are thought to have watched on television. Twelve people have walked on the Moon, all between 1969 and 1972.

The race gradually gave way to cooperation. In 1975 an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked in orbit, and their commanders shook hands through the hatch. Since November 2000 the International Space Station, built by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, has been continuously inhabited — meaning that for over two decades, there has always been someone living off the planet.

Spain has its own place in the story. In 1998 Pedro Duque became the first Spanish astronaut, flying aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, and later visited the International Space Station. Today, rockets land themselves on barges, space telescopes look back almost to the beginning of the universe, and new missions are heading for the Moon again. Look up on a clear night from Tibidabo, and you may see the station glide silently overhead.

lb_haiku.title: Seventeen Syllables: The Art of Haiku
lb_haiku.author: Yoko Tanaka i Mir
lb_haiku.desc: The short Japanese poem, its masters, and original haiku written in Barcelona. Library copy; do not remove.
text: A haiku is a very short poem, traditionally of seventeen sound units arranged five, seven, five. The Japanese count not syllables exactly but 'on', or morae, so English haiku that obey the 5-7-5 rule are only an approximation — and many modern poets ignore it altogether. More important than the counting is the cut, the kireji, a pause that sets two images side by side, and the kigo, a word that anchors the poem in a season: frogs for spring, cicadas for summer, the moon for autumn.

The form grew out of the opening verse of linked poems composed by groups of poets in turn. Matsuo Bashō, in the seventeenth century, raised it to an art. His most famous poem, written in 1686, describes an old pond, a frog jumping in, and the sound of the water. In a rough version of my own: 'The old pond — / a frog leaps in: / the sound of water.' That is all. Generations of readers have found in those few words the whole of stillness broken and restored.

Later masters took the form in their own directions. Yosa Buson was also a painter, and his haiku are vivid pictures. Kobayashi Issa wrote with great tenderness for small creatures — flies, snails, sparrows — and for the sorrows of his own life, which were many. Masaoka Shiki, at the end of the nineteenth century, gave the form its modern name, 'haiku', and urged poets to sketch directly from life.

Here are some haiku written for this library, in the spirit of Shiki's advice to sketch from life.

  Tram bell on the hill —
  the whole Eixample below
  folding into dusk.

  Low tide at Barceloneta:
  a child digs for the whole sea
  with a yellow spade.

  Library, late May.
  Someone's deadline turns a page;
  the fan turns its head.

And two more, for the seasons of the city.

  First autumn thunder —
  on every Rambla awning
  a thousand small drums.

  Sant Jordi evening:
  a rose in one hand, a book
  open in the other.

Write your own. Count if it helps, stop counting when it doesn't, and look very carefully at one small thing. That is the whole of the method, and it takes a lifetime.

lb_poetry.title: Fourteen Lines and Other Cages: Poetry Forms of the World
lb_poetry.author: Dr. Martí Lloret & Dr. Nour Haddad
lb_poetry.desc: Sonnets, ghazals, villanelles and more, with original examples of each. Library copy; do not remove.
text: Poets have always built themselves cages in order to sing in them. A form — a fixed number of lines, a pattern of rhyme or rhythm — seems like a limitation, but it often gives a poem its power, forcing the poet to find a better word than the first one that came. This book collects some of the world's great forms, with a small original example of each, written for students who are allowed to groan.

The sonnet was perfected in fourteenth-century Italy by Petrarch: fourteen lines, an octave that poses a problem and a sestet that turns to answer it. In England, Shakespeare's version ends with a rhyming couplet that snaps shut like a box. A short sonnet-sketch:

  I came here with a suitcase and a map,
  a timetable, a phrasebook and a plan;
  the city laughed and stole them for a nap
  and gave me back a café and a fan.

We leave the other ten lines as an exercise.

The ghazal, developed in Arabic and brought to perfection in Persian by poets such as Hafez, is made of self-contained couplets linked by a repeated word or phrase, the radif, at the end of each second line. Traditionally the poet names himself in the final couplet. An example, with 'by the sea' as its radif:

  All my lost afternoons are waiting by the sea;
  the gulls keep careful accounts by the sea.
  Sandra, put down the textbook for an hour —
  the best economics is taught by the sea.

The villanelle has nineteen lines and only two rhymes, and two refrains that return again and again, which makes it ideal for obsessions. The Japanese tanka, older than the haiku, has five lines in a 5-7-5-7-7 pattern. And the limerick, that English cousin of nonsense, has five lines and a bouncing rhythm:

  A student who studied in Spain
  found the timetable hard to explain:
  she had lunch at half-three,
  then went down to the sea,
  and returned just in time for the train.

Catalan poetry has its own proud tradition, from the medieval troubadours to Ausiàs March in fifteenth-century Valencia and the great twentieth-century poets such as Salvador Espriu and Mercè Rodoreda, better known as a novelist. The Jocs Florals, poetry contests revived in Barcelona in 1859, awarded a real flower — a natural rose — as one of their prizes. Choose a form, break it gently, and write something true. The cage, you will find, has a door.

note1.title: Study Notes 1: Supply & Demand
note1.desc: Chapter 1 of the legendary UPF study guide: supply, demand and the magic of equilibrium. Photocopied so often the margins have gone grey.
text: THE RAMBLA GUIDE TO ECONOMICS — CHAPTER 1: SUPPLY & DEMAND. Compiled by generations of UPF students who could not afford the textbook, annotated by generations more who could not read each other's handwriting. If you have found this page, congratulations: you are now part of an unbroken chain of borrowed knowledge. Please do not spill coffee on it. Everyone else already has.

Every market in the world, from the Boqueria to the stock exchange, is a tug of war between two groups of people. Buyers want to pay less; sellers want to be paid more. Economists draw these two desires as curves, and then — this is the entire trick of the subject — look for where they cross.

DEMAND first. Imagine ice creams on the beach at Barceloneta. When they are expensive, few people buy; when they are cheap, everyone suddenly remembers they love pistachio. The quantity demanded falls as the price rises. This is the law of demand, and unlike most laws in this city, it is almost always obeyed.

SUPPLY next. The ice-cream sellers behave the other way round. At a high price it is worth dragging another freezer across the sand; at a low price they would rather sit in the shade. The quantity supplied rises as the price rises. Buyers and sellers are, in a sense, reading the same price tag and drawing opposite conclusions.

Now some numbers, because the exam will have numbers. Suppose the daily demand for ice creams on one stretch of beach is:

      Qd = 120 − 15P

where P is the price in euros. At €2, Qd = 120 − 30 = 90 ice creams; at €4, only 60. And suppose supply is:

      Qs = 30P

so at €2 the sellers offer 60, and at €4 they offer 120.

At €2 buyers want 90 but only 60 are on offer: a shortage, queues, grumbling, and the price creeps up. At €4 sellers offer 120 but only 60 are wanted: a surplus, melting stock, and the price creeps down. Somewhere in between there is a price where the queue and the melting both stop. We call it EQUILIBRIUM, and we find it by setting demand equal to supply.

Set Qd = Qs:

      120 − 15P = 30P
      120 = 45P
      P* = 120 ÷ 45 ≈ €2.67

Now put the price back into either equation:

      Q* = 30 × 2.67 ≈ 80   (exactly 80 if you keep the fraction 8/3)

So the market settles at about €2.67 per ice cream, with 80 sold a day. Every buyer who values an ice cream at €2.67 or more gets one, and every seller willing to sell at that price sells.

Nobody on the beach knows these equations, of course. Nobody needs to. The price does the work, rising when there are too few ice creams and falling when there are too many, like a very patient waiter who never takes a tip. This is what Adam Smith was getting at, and it is honestly rather beautiful when you think about it at 2 a.m. before an exam.
A final warning from previous students: do not confuse the price with the quantity. Every year someone writes 'the equilibrium quantity is 2.67 ice creams', which is a very sad amount of ice cream.
Remember for the exam: equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — with Qd = 120 − 15P and Qs = 30P, the price is about €2.67 and the equilibrium QUANTITY is 80.

note2.title: Study Notes 2: Opportunity Cost
note2.desc: Chapter 2 of the legendary UPF study guide: the true price of everything, including a day at the beach. Maria's own copy, colour-coded.
text: THE RAMBLA GUIDE TO ECONOMICS — CHAPTER 2: OPPORTUNITY COST. This chapter will ruin every free thing you have ever enjoyed. You have been warned. (Previous owner's note in green ink: 'It did. Worth it.')

Economists have a slightly irritating habit of pointing out that nothing is free. Not because someone is secretly charging you, but because every choice means giving up something else. Your time, your money and your attention are all limited. Spend them here and you cannot spend them there.

The OPPORTUNITY COST of a choice is the value of the best alternative you give up to make it. Not all the alternatives — just the best one. If you could have gone to the cinema, to the library, or to work, and you went to the beach, the opportunity cost of the beach is whichever of those three you would have picked next.

Let us do it with numbers, since the examiners are fond of this one. Imagine you have a part-time job at a café that pays €8 an hour, and you could work a six-hour shift on Saturday. Instead you spend those six hours at the beach, which has no entrance fee and is, as everyone keeps telling you, free.

It is not free. The opportunity cost of your beach day is the wage you gave up:

      opportunity cost = hours × wage
      = 6 h × €8/h
      = €48

That is the true price of your beach day. You did not hand anyone €48; you simply did not receive it. Economists count both.

This does not mean you should not have gone to the beach. If the sun, the swim and the sardines were worth more than €48 to you, it was an excellent decision. Opportunity cost is not a scolding; it is a measuring stick. It asks, very politely, 'was it worth it?'

It also explains a great deal of human behaviour. Why do busy professionals pay someone to clean their flat? Because an hour of their time is worth more than the cleaner's fee. Why do students queue for an hour for free concert tickets while their parents simply buy them? Because the student's hour costs less. Everyone is weighing their own opportunity costs, even if they have never heard the phrase.

A classic trap: money already spent and gone for good — a 'sunk cost' — is not an opportunity cost. If you bought a non-refundable ticket for a boring film, the money is gone whether you stay or leave. The only question is what else you could be doing with the next two hours.
Remember for the exam: the opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the best alternative given up — six hours at the beach instead of working at €8 an hour costs 6 × €8 = €48.

note3.title: Study Notes 3: The Economics of the Grid
note3.desc: Chapter 3 of the legendary UPF study guide: land, public space and Cerdà's chamfered blocks. Slightly chewed. Retrieved by a very good dog.
text: THE RAMBLA GUIDE TO ECONOMICS — CHAPTER 3: THE ECONOMICS OF THE GRID. This chapter is about land, which is the one thing they are genuinely not making any more of. (Note from a previous owner: 'Read it walking round the Eixample. It makes much more sense on foot.')

Land is special in economics because its supply is fixed. You can bake more bread, print more books and brew more coffee, but you cannot manufacture another square metre of central Barcelona. When demand for a fixed supply rises, only one thing can move: the price. This is why a flat on the Passeig de Gràcia costs roughly as much as a small Pyrenean village.

When Ildefons Cerdà drew the Eixample in the 1850s, he was making an economic choice about how to divide scarce land between private buildings and public space. Streets, squares and those famous chamfered corners are land that nobody can build on, given to everyone. Every tile of pavement is a tile of flat that was never built.

Let us measure it, because the exam will. Model a block as a square of s × s tiles, and cut off each of the four corners with a diagonal c tiles deep. Each cut corner removes a small staircase-shaped triangle of c(c + 1)/2 tiles, and there are four of them, so:

      A = s² − 4 × c(c + 1)/2
      A = s² − 2c(c + 1)

Now use the real game-sized block: s = 9, c = 2.

      A = 9² − 2 × 2 × (2 + 1)
      A = 81 − 12
      A = 69 tiles

So a 9 × 9 block chamfered two tiles deep has 69 tiles of built area, and 12 tiles — about fifteen per cent — handed over to the corner plazas. Go and count one if you do not believe us. Previous students have, and several were questioned by the Guàrdia Urbana.

Why would a city deliberately give away fifteen per cent of its most valuable land? Because the chamfers create something the market alone would under-supply: a PUBLIC GOOD. Light, visibility at crossroads, space for carts, café terraces, a place for a newspaper kiosk and a bench. Nobody can be excluded from enjoying a corner plaza, and one person's enjoyment of it does not use it up — the two classic features of a public good.

Markets are excellent at providing things people can buy one at a time, like ice creams. They are poor at providing things everyone shares, because each person hopes someone else will pay — the 'free-rider problem'. That is why pavements, parks and lighthouses are usually paid for collectively, through taxes, rather than sold one sunset at a time.

Cerdà wanted even more: blocks built on only two sides, with gardens in the middle. Developers, facing the high price of land, filled the blocks in on all four sides instead, because each extra square metre built was worth more to them privately than the garden was. It is a textbook case of private incentives and public good pulling in different directions. The city is still, slowly, buying the gardens back.
Remember for the exam: a 9 × 9 Eixample block chamfered two tiles deep has A = s² − 2c(c + 1) = 81 − 12 = 69 tiles of built area.

note4.title: Study Notes 4: Incentives & the Deposit Bottle
note4.desc: Chapter 4 of the legendary UPF study guide: why people do what they do, explained with a single empty bottle. Found pressed in a paperback.
text: THE RAMBLA GUIDE TO ECONOMICS — CHAPTER 4: INCENTIVES. If economics has one sentence you should tattoo somewhere discreet, it is this: people respond to incentives. (Previous owner: 'Do not actually tattoo it. Ask me how I know.')

An incentive is anything that changes the costs or benefits of a choice. Prices are incentives; so are fines, rewards, deadlines, praise and the threat of your flatmate's disapproval. Change the incentives and, very often, you change the behaviour, whether or not anyone gives a speech about it.

Consider the humble empty bottle. Without any incentive, a bottle finished on the beach is worth nothing to the person holding it. Carrying it to a recycling point takes a little effort, so many bottles end up in the sand or the sea. Everyone agrees this is a pity, and the bottles keep appearing anyway.

Now add a DEPOSIT. You pay a little extra when you buy the drink, and you get it back when you return the empty. Germany has run such a system — the Pfand — for years, and returning bottles has become almost a national reflex. Suddenly the empty bottle is not rubbish. It is a coin with a neck.

The decision can be written as a very small inequality. Let d be the deposit and e the effort cost of returning the bottle — your time and trouble, measured in euros. A rational person returns the bottle if and only if:

      d > e

With a deposit of €1.00 and an effort cost of, say, €0.20:

      €1.00 > €0.20   →   return the bottle.

If the deposit were only €0.05, the inequality would flip for many people, and the bottle would stay on the beach.

Notice something lovely: even the people who do not bother to return their bottles now leave behind something valuable. Other people pick them up. The deposit does not only change the behaviour of the drinker; it creates a whole informal army of collectors, who clean the streets and earn a little money doing it. One small incentive, two benefits.

Incentives can also backfire. A famous story tells of a colonial government that paid a bounty for dead cobras to reduce their number — and people began breeding cobras to collect the bounty. When the scheme was cancelled, the breeders released their now-worthless snakes, and there were more cobras than before. Economists call such surprises 'perverse incentives'. Always ask what a rule will really make people do.
Remember for the exam: a rational person returns a deposit bottle if and only if the deposit is greater than the effort cost, d > e — at €1.00 against €0.20, return it.

note5.title: Study Notes 5: Comparative Advantage
note5.desc: Chapter 5 of the legendary UPF study guide: why fishermen should fish and bakers should bake. Faintly salty. Blown in on the sea wind.
text: THE RAMBLA GUIDE TO ECONOMICS — CHAPTER 5: COMPARATIVE ADVANTAGE. This is the most important idea in the whole guide, and the one most people get wrong at dinner parties. Read it twice. (Previous owner: 'Read it three times. Still worth it.')

In 1817 David Ricardo showed something that sounds impossible: two people can both gain from trade even if one of them is better at everything. The trick is that what matters is not who is best at a task, but who gives up the least to do it. That is COMPARATIVE advantage, as opposed to absolute advantage, and the difference is the whole game.

Our characters: a fisherman and a baker on the Barcelona waterfront. In one day, the fisherman can either catch 12 fish or bake 2 loaves. The baker can either catch 4 fish or bake 8 loaves. The fisherman is better at fishing, the baker is better at baking — so far, so obvious. But let us measure the cost properly.

The opportunity cost of a loaf is the fish you give up to bake it. For the fisherman, two loaves cost a whole day of fishing, twelve fish, so each loaf costs:

      12 ÷ 2 = 6 fish per loaf

For the baker, eight loaves cost four fish, so each loaf costs:

      4 ÷ 8 = 0.5 fish per loaf

A loaf costs the fisherman twelve times as much as it costs the baker.

Turn it around for fish. For the fisherman, one fish costs 2 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.17 loaves. For the baker, one fish costs 8 ÷ 4 = 2 loaves. So the fisherman has the lower opportunity cost in fish, and the baker has the lower opportunity cost in bread. Each should specialise in the thing they give up least to produce.

If they each work alone and split their time, they both end up with a little of each and a lot of tiredness. If the fisherman fishes all day and the baker bakes all day, together they produce 12 fish and 8 loaves — and by trading at any rate between 0.5 and 6 fish per loaf, BOTH can end up with more of both than they could have made alone. Nobody was robbed. The extra came from specialisation.

Now the surprising case. Suppose the baker were better at everything — faster at fishing AND at baking. Ricardo's insight still holds: as long as their opportunity costs differ, each has a comparative advantage in something, and trade still helps both. This is why a brilliant economist might still pay someone else to fix her bicycle.

Comparative advantage explains why countries trade, why flatmates divide chores, and why you should probably let the person who enjoys cooking do the cooking while you do the washing-up. It does not explain who should choose the music. Some problems are beyond economics.

Remember for the exam: specialise where your opportunity cost is lowest — a loaf costs the fisherman 12/2 = 6 fish but the baker only 4/8 = 0.5 fish, so the BAKER should bake and the fisherman should fish.

EXAM.q: Question 1 of 5. Demand is Qd = 120 − 15P and supply is Qs = 30P. What is the equilibrium QUANTITY?
Question 2 of 5. You spend six hours at the beach instead of working at €8 an hour. What is the opportunity cost of your beach day?
Question 3 of 5. How many tiles of built area does a 9 × 9 Eixample block, chamfered two tiles deep at each corner, have?
Question 4 of 5. Under a deposit scheme, when does a rational person return an empty bottle?
a: When the deposit exceeds the effort cost
Never — it is a sunk cost
EXAM.ok: When the deposit exceeds the effort cost

EXAM.q: Question 5 of 5. A fisherman can catch 12 fish or bake 2 loaves a day; a baker can catch 4 fish or bake 8 loaves. Who should bake the bread?
a: The baker — a loaf costs her only 0.5 fish
EXAM.ok: The baker — a loaf costs her only 0.5 fish

rosa.name: Rosa
rosa.intro: I'm Rosa — born in Tarragona, Barcelona by choice, your flatmate, and the one who waters the plants you forget.
lines: Barcelona has more than four kilometres of beaches, and most of its seafront was rebuilt for the 1992 Olympics. Before that it was railway tracks and warehouses.
Press J for your journal — it keeps track of everything you're doing. And M shows the map, if you're like me and turn left when you mean right.
Flor del Iliri means 'lily flower'. Our little street is just off La Rambla, which makes the rent tragic and the location perfect.

alessandra.name: Alessandra
alessandra.intro: Alessandra! Dancer, party-thrower, birthday girl — and the reason you'll never get to bed before two in this city.
lines: La Mercè, the city's great festival, fills the end of September: castellers, giants, fireworks, and the correfoc, where devils run through the streets with sparklers. I have the scorched shirt to prove it.
If you're flagging, eat something from your bag — you'll feel a real spring in your step for a little while.
Passeig de Gràcia was a country road to the village of Gràcia before the Eixample swallowed it. Now it's all Gaudí, fancy shops — and me.
birthday: I'm still eating your torró — one tiny square a day, to make it last. I've told everyone it was the best present. Don't tell my mother.
Clara sent me forty-one photos from the party. In thirty-nine I'm mid-dance. In the other two I'm mid-sentence.
Someone left a paper party hat on my bookshelf. I'm keeping it there. It's a monument now.
My neighbour asked if the party was a wedding. I told her no — just a birthday, done properly.
You know Catalans tug the birthday girl's ears, once for every year? Iker took that tradition far too literally.
Next birthday: a boat, a band, and you in charge of the torró again. It's decided. I've written it down.
exam: Don't study too hard, Sandra! Leave time to dance — exams aren't for ages yet, and Barcelona won't dance with itself.
You've danced through most of this city by now. Maybe... it's time to study? I can't believe I just said that.
YOU PASSED! Tonight we dance on the tables. Carefully. Metaphorically. No — actually.

alice.name: Alice
alice.intro: Alice — medical student, professional hypochondriac, and currently, genuinely, very sniffly. Don't come too close.
lines: The Chupa Chups lollipop was invented near here in 1958 by Enric Bernat, and Salvador Dalí designed the daisy logo. I'm eating my way through the evidence.
Cupboards and drawers are storage too — if your bag gets full, leave things in a cupboard and come back for them later.
Carrer de Balmes is named after Jaume Balmes, a nineteenth-century philosopher. It's also a very long walk uphill, which is why I'm lying down.
exam: Doctor's orders — and I'm the doctor now: see the sights, don't bury yourself in books. The exam isn't for ages.
Sounds like you've seen most of the city. As your doctor, I now prescribe studying. Twice daily, with water.
Congratulations, Dr. Sandra! I feel better already. It must be contagious.

alba.name: Alba
alba.intro: I'm Alba! I study biology, I press flowers, and I live across from the Ciutadella so I can pretend the whole park is my garden.
lines: Barcelona is full of wild green parakeets — monk parakeets. They escaped from pet shops decades ago, and now they run the palm trees.
Wildflowers grow back on the grass whenever you pop inside somewhere and come out again. Nature is generous like that.
The Ciutadella was a fortress built to watch over the city after 1714. When it came down, Barcelona turned it into a park — the best revenge.
exam: Look at that light outside! Don't waste it on textbooks — exams aren't for a long time yet.
You've seen most of Barcelona by now, haven't you? Maybe it's time for the library, before the light fades.
You passed! I'm pressing a flower for you. It'll be ready in three weeks. Science is slow.

maria.name: Maria
maria.intro: Maria. Economics, second year, UPF. I colour-code my notes and I am not ashamed.
lines: Cerdà's Eixample blocks are about 113 metres on each side and the streets twenty metres wide. I once measured ours in footsteps. Don't ask.
Money in this city comes three ways: coins on the ground, deposit bottles, and people who are grateful. Use all three.
Carrer d'Aragó had a railway running along it in an open trench until the 1960s. They covered it over and put the traffic on top.
exam: Marginal utility of one more hour of study right now: low. Of one more afternoon exploring: high. Rationally, go outside. The exam isn't for a while.
You've explored most of the city — diminishing returns have set in. The marginal hour of study is now worth more. Time to study.
You passed. I've updated my spreadsheet of people I'm proud of. You're at the top, in green.

empar.name: Empar
lines: Crema catalana is traditionally eaten on 19 March, the feast of Sant Josep. We serve it every day. Sant Josep would understand.
Our crema catalana is the finest in Barcelona — the sugar is torched to order, right in front of you. That is why it costs €15. Quality is never an accident.
La Rambla was once a dry riverbed along the old city wall — the name comes from the Arabic 'ramla', sand.

jaume.name: Jaume
lines: Barcelona's first metro line opened in 1924. My grandfather rode it on the first day and complained about it for fifty years.
If you want a quiet coffee, go to Cafè Berlín up in the north. If you want gossip, stay here with me.
Cafés here put their tables on the pavement the moment the sun comes out. The terrassa is sacred.

ferran.name: Ferran
ferran.intro: Ferran, baker. I studied in Munich for two years and came home with a sourdough starter and a completely unreasonable love of rye.
lines: On the night of Sant Joan in June, everyone in Catalonia eats coca de Sant Joan — a flat sweet bread with candied fruit and pine nuts.
I sell Vollkornbrot, genuine German rye bread. A novelty here, I know — but my homesick regulars would riot without it.
Up here near the Diagonal you're close to Gràcia, the old village with its own festa major every August, when whole streets are decorated by the neighbours.

joan.name: Joan
joan.intro: Joan, third generation of Casa Joan. My grandfather toasted almonds on this very spot when the Rambla still had horses.
lines: The most famous torrons come from Xixona and Alacant, but Agramunt, here in Catalonia, makes a wonderful one too.
Torró is €12 a bar. Not cheap, but it's a proper gift — people remember a good torró long after they forget a bunch of flowers.
La Rambla is really five Ramblas end to end, each with its own name: Canaletes, Estudis, Sant Josep, Caputxins and Santa Mònica.

neus.name: Neus
lines: Barcelona gets something like 2,500 hours of sunshine a year — which is why my torró lives in the back, in the shade.
Salva the beachcomber buys seashells — all of them at once. He's usually on the eastern end of the beach.
The Gran Via de les Corts Catalanes is one of the longest streets in Spain, around thirteen kilometres from end to end.

xavi.name: Xavi
lines: Barcelona has around forty municipal food markets. La Boqueria is only the most famous — every neighbourhood has its own.
Everyday snacks are a euro or two here. Save your big money for gifts.
The Gran Via marks the edge of the Eixample; below it the city tumbles down towards the old districts and the sea.

anna.name: Anna
lines: Barcelona sorts its rubbish into colours: yellow for plastic and cans, blue for paper, green for glass, brown for food scraps.
Bring me every empty bottle you find. The beach is full of them and they come back after a while — and the street bins sometimes hide one.
This is the Pfand refund desk: every bottle, one euro. It works just like the deposit system in Germany — you'll know the drill better than I do.

ponc.name: Ponç
ponc.intro: Ponç. I sell books. I have sold books in this shop for thirty years, and I have been looking for one particular book for twenty-nine of them.
lines: On Sant Jordi, 23 April, Barcelona sells well over a million books in a single day. I sleep for the whole of the 24th.
If you want to read without buying, the university library at UPF is free — first floor, up the big staircase. Tell Remei I sent you.
Cerdà wanted a garden in the middle of every block. Ours has a fig tree that has outlived three landlords.

oriol.name: Prof. Oriol
oriol.intro: Professor Oriol Casanovas, Microeconomics. Welcome to the department. Mind the stack of working papers by the door — it bites.
lines: Universitat Pompeu Fabra was founded in 1990, which makes it a teenager among universities. The University of Barcelona dates from 1450.
The library is upstairs; the double staircase is in the corner, with the sign beside it. Several first-years have still managed to miss it.
This campus was once a military barracks. We replaced the drilling with lectures, which some students say is no improvement.

pol.name: Pol
lines: Pompeu Fabra, the linguist our university is named after, trained as an engineer before he fixed the spelling of modern Catalan.
Prof. Oriol is always in the lecture hall. Always. I'm not certain he has a home.
The university library is in an old water reservoir — the Dipòsit de les Aigües. Brick arches everywhere. It's gorgeous.

remei.name: Remei
lines: Barcelona has around forty public libraries, and every one of them will lend you a book for nothing but a promise.
You may read any book on these shelves, for as long as you like. Taking one away, however, is another matter entirely.
Welcome to the reading room. Please whisper. The silence up here is load-bearing.

cesc.name: Cesc
