lines: In Catalan a 'biblioteca' is a library and a 'llibreria' is a bookshop. Mix them up and you'll try to borrow from a shop.
In a bookshelf, press R to read the book you've got selected. You'll be here for hours. I have been here for hours.
This floor holds the world collection: Japan to Sweden, the Silk Road to the space race. I'm on Keynes versus Hayek. It's a rap battle, basically.

pau.name: Pau
pau.intro: Pau. Stonemason. Forty years carving this basilica, and I'll probably carve for forty more — it's that kind of building.
lines: Gaudí is buried in the crypt beneath us. In his last years he practically lived here, among the plaster models.
Talk to everyone. Half this city has a problem you could solve, and the other half has advice.
When it's finished there will be eighteen towers: twelve for the apostles, four for the evangelists, one for Mary, and the tallest of all for Jesus.

merce.name: Mercè
lines: The Nativity façade faces east, towards the sunrise; the Passion façade faces west, towards the sunset.
Every landmark has a plaque beside its door. Read all ten and you'll know this city better than most guides — and I am a guide.
Look at the windows: cool blues and greens on the east side, warm reds and golds on the west. At sunset the whole nave glows.

carme.name: Carme
carme.intro: Carme Ferrer, conservator. I spend my days with twelfth-century saints, a magnifying lamp and very small brushes.
lines: The Romanesque murals here were lifted from Pyrenean churches around 1920 to stop them being sold abroad, piece by piece.
The museum café does a lovely cafè amb llet. Stop in if you're passing — art is thirsty work.
The Palau Nacional was built for the 1929 International Exhibition, and so was the Magic Fountain at the foot of its steps.

joaquim.name: Joaquim
lines: The Magic Fountain of Montjuïc was designed by Carles Buïgas for the 1929 Exhibition. It still dances on summer evenings.
Don't touch the frescoes. Do look at them — for a long time. That's the whole trick of museums.
The apse of Sant Climent de Taüll, consecrated in 1123, shows Christ in Majesty. The original is here; the little church keeps a copy.

lluisa.name: Lluïsa
lines: The 'Block of Discord' on the Passeig de Gràcia puts buildings by Gaudí, Domènech i Montaner and Puig i Cadafalch side by side.
Missions come to you by talking. Anyone with a worried face might need a hand.
The tiles of the light well get darker blue as they rise, so the daylight feels even from top to bottom. Gaudí thought of everything.

ramon.name: Ramon
lines: Casa Milà has no load-bearing interior walls — pillars and iron beams carry it, so the rooms could be shaped however the owners liked.
If you have a bike, press B to ride. Just not on the sand, and certainly not in here.
The roof has twenty-eight chimneys and vents. Some people swear the helmeted ones inspired a certain galactic villain.

eulalia.name: Eulàlia
lines: Gaudí designed Casa Vicens when he was barely thirty. It was his first big commission, and you can feel him showing off.
Always open cupboards. People forget the strangest things in them — umbrellas, hats, cameras, whole afternoons.
The yellow flowers on the tiles are marigolds. The story goes that they were growing on the plot when Gaudí first came to see it.

enric.name: Enric
lines: The Calvet family ran their textile business on the ground floor and lived upstairs — very Barcelona.
The street plaques on the corner lamp posts tell you where you are. Read a few and the grid starts to make sense.
The carved mushrooms over the door are there because the family loved mycology. It's the only front door in town that doubles as a field guide.

teresa.name: Teresa
lines: Eusebi Güell was Gaudí's greatest patron — he also commissioned Park Güell and the crypt at the Colònia Güell.
Look up in here too: the central hall rises to a dome pierced with little holes, like stars in a night sky.
There's an organ built into the central hall. When it plays, the whole house hums along.

montse.name: Montse
montse.intro: I'm Montse. I've lived above a bakery on this Rambla for thirty-one years, and I've walked it every evening of my life with my little dog.
lines: The Canaletes fountain at the top of the Rambla has a legend: drink from it and you'll always come back to Barcelona.
Watch your pockets on the Rambla. Not everyone who smiles at you is as nice as they look.
Joan Miró designed the round mosaic set into the Rambla pavement in 1976. Thousands walk over it every day without noticing.

manolo.name: Manolo
lines: Hola, hola, guapa! Welcome, welcome! La Rambla is over a kilometre long, and I have walked every centimetre of it, many times, very carefully.
A tip, from a friend — because we are friends now: watch out for pickpockets round here. Terrible people. Keep your bag close. Closer. Perfect.
Ah, La Rambla! Poets, painters, flower sellers — and so many visitors, so relaxed, so trusting. A beautiful place to... work.

bofarull.name: Agent Bofarull
lines: The Guàrdia Urbana is Barcelona's city police: traffic, noise, lost tourists, and people who think the fountain is a swimming pool.
A friendly word: be wary of charming strangers on the Rambla. If someone is too nice, too fast, check your bag.
This is the Font de Canaletes. When Barça win something big, thousands of fans celebrate right here. I'm usually standing exactly where you are.

gloria.name: Glòria
lines: There have been flower stalls on the Rambla for well over a century. This stretch is still called the Rambla de les Flors.
Wildflowers grow in the grass — the green band under the mountains, the riverbank, the forest. Never on the pavement, maca!
The Boqueria market is just behind these stalls: fruit piled like jewels and the best fresh juice in the city.

iu.name: Iu
lines: (The bronze statue winks.) Living statues have been part of the Rambla for decades. The city licenses us now. Very official.
(Without moving his lips:) Press M. Look at the map. I've been standing here for nine hours; trust me, I know where everything is.
(A whisper:) This is the middle of the Rambla. Every visitor in the city passes me eventually. I see everything. I say nothing. Mostly.

pere.name: Pere
lines: Every Barcelona postcode starts with 08. This whole Eixample is 080-something. I could recite them in my sleep. I do, apparently.
Lost? Find the Rambla. It runs from the mountains all the way down to the sea, straight as a letter.
I deliver to every door on this stretch. Flor del Iliri, 4? SANDRA & ROSA, little German flag. I never forget a doorbell.

dolors.name: Dolors
lines: Barcelona has more than seventy public parks. I have sat on a bench in most of them.
The Pfand desk at Carrefour takes empty bottles, a euro each. My grandson paid for his bicycle that way.
The Rambla runs straight down to the sea. Just keep walking downhill — it's the only direction every Barcelonan agrees on.

lluis.name: Lluís
lines: The Rambla's stalls once sold everything: papers, flowers, even songbirds on one stretch, in the old days.
Journal's J, map's M, bag's I. I sell paper maps, but honestly, the M key is free.
La Vanguardia, one of the city's big newspapers, has been printed in Barcelona since 1881.

jordi.name: Jordi
jordi.intro: Bon dia! Jordi. I fix bikes — on this bit of pavement, rain or shine, since before Bicing was a twinkle in the mayor's eye.
lines: Barcelona's Bicing shared bikes arrived in 2007. I fixed half of them the first month.
With a bike you're three times faster — but no riding on the sand, the chain hates it, and none indoors.
Aragó had a railway running down it in an open trench until the 1960s. They covered it and put the traffic on top.

marta.name: Marta
marta.intro: Hi! Marta — photographer, from Seville, and I've been staring at this building for an hour like it owes me money.
lines: Casa Batlló's façade is covered in trencadís — broken glass and ceramic — so it shimmers like the surface of the sea.
Take pictures of everything. Memory is good; memory plus a photograph is better.
Look at those balconies — people call them masks, or skulls. They call the whole house the House of Bones.

vicenc.name: Vicenç
lines: When I was a boy, the Eixample's inner courtyards were full of workshops. Now they're opening them into gardens again, one at a time.
The rubbish bins stand on the pavements by the plain blocks. Keep the city tidy — and sometimes somebody's left a bottle in there worth a euro.
Passeig de Gràcia is paved with Gaudí's hexagonal tiles, with sea creatures pressed into them: a starfish, an octopus, an ammonite.

angel.name: Àngel
lines: Barcelona is trying 'superilles' — superblocks — where cars are kept out of groups of streets and the crossroads become little plazas.
If a snack gives you a burst of energy, you'll see a small card down in the corner. My dogs get the same effect from one biscuit.
Roger de Llúria was a medieval admiral of the Crown of Aragon, one of the most feared commanders at sea in his day.

silvia.name: Sílvia
lines: Pa amb tomàquet — bread rubbed with tomato, oil and salt — is the Catalan answer to every question asked before noon.
Supermarket snacks are a euro or two. Don't let anyone sell you a banana for more.
Carrer de Girona is named after the city of Girona, up north, with its colourful houses hanging over the river Onyar.

nerea.name: Nerea
lines: Avinguda Diagonal cuts across the whole grid at an angle — one of the few streets Cerdà allowed to break the pattern.
The mountains are north, the sea south, the forest east and the river west. If you can't find something, it's probably east.
From the Diagonal you can see Tibidabo on the hill. The funicular station is at the foot of the path — I run up there on Sundays. Slowly.

albert.name: Albert
lines: The afternoon wind off the sea is called the 'marinada'. It's why kites fly so well over Barcelona.
Wildflowers love this grass under the mountains. Pick them — they grow back.
From this strip of grass you can see the whole skyline: Tibidabo behind, the Sagrada spires, and the sea beyond the city.

salva.name: Salva
lines: Barceloneta was built in the eighteenth century for families who lost their homes when the Ciutadella fortress went up.
I buy seashells — all of them at once, a euro apiece. They wash up on this eastern beach, and fresh ones come in every tide or two.
The sea here is nearly tideless — a few centimetres, no more. That's why the shells land in the same few places every day.

tomas.name: Tomàs
lines: Fishing boats still work out of Barcelona's port, and the fish auction there starts well before dawn.
Núria is always telling people where to look for things. Listen to her; she gets it from her grandmother.
From this spot you can watch the city wake up: the mountains go pink first, then the towers, then the sea.

nuria.name: Núria
nuria.intro: Hi, I'm Núria! I'm on holiday from university, keeping my grandfather company while he fishes. And talks to the fish.
lines: The Olympic Port was built for the 1992 sailing events, along with the two tall towers beside it — still the tallest buildings in the city.
If you find something someone has lost, bring it back to them. People in this city have long memories for kindness.
Avi Tomàs has fished from this spot since before I was born. He says the fish know him. The fish do not know him.

quima.name: Quima
lines: The Barcelona seafront is about ten beaches in a row, each with its own personality. This one is the sociable one.
Bottles wash up on the western half of the beach and shells on the eastern. It's as if the sea sorts its own recycling.
In summer this sand is full by eleven. In September it's perfect — warm sea, fewer people, long golden evenings.

bernat.name: Bernat
lines: The Mediterranean off Barcelona is warmest in August, when it can reach 25 °C or more.
No swimming out past the waves — and no bikes on the sand. Walk it, like a civilised person.
Those are yellow-legged gulls. Never eat a sandwich near them. They have absolutely no shame.

oscar.name: Òscar
lines: The city zoo is inside this park. Its famous white gorilla, Floquet de Neu — Snowflake — lived there until 2003.
The Cascada fountain is at the north end of the park. Lost things always seem to end up in the grass around it.
This park hosted the 1888 Universal Exhibition. The Arc de Triomf up the road was built as its grand gateway.

mireia.name: Mireia
lines: The Parliament of Catalonia meets inside this park, in the old arsenal of the citadel.
A snack gives you a lovely burst of energy for a little while. Eat another and it simply starts over — it doesn't stack.
There's a life-size stone mammoth in this park, from 1907. Nobody quite knows why. Everybody loves it.

roser.name: Roser
lines: Collserola is home to holm oaks, Aleppo pines and wild boar — the boar sometimes wander into the city's streets at night.
I buy wildflowers, all you have, a euro each. They grow on the grass and come back whenever you've been indoors a while.
This forest is full of rosemary, thyme and wild fennel. Rub a leaf between your fingers — that's the smell of Catalonia.

guillem.name: Guillem
lines: Catalans are mad for wild mushrooms. 'Anar a buscar bolets' — going mushroom-hunting — is practically an autumn religion.
The forest has clearings and old tracks. If you can't get through somewhere, try the paths running east from the city streets.
Never eat a mushroom you can't name with total certainty. I've hunted for forty years and I still carry the book.

genis.name: Genís
lines: The Tibidabo funicular opened in 1901, one of the first in Spain. It still creaks up the hill like a patient old goat.
The steps up to Tibidabo climb straight up the hill from here. Take them slowly and look back at the city now and then.
The Tramvia Blau, the old Blue Tram, used to meet the funicular down here — one of the city's oldest tram lines.

arnau.name: Arnau
lines: The Avió, a replica aeroplane ride from 1928, still flies in circles over the city. Nobody has ever landed it. That's the point.
The whole city is visible from this terrace. Use your map if you can't tell which tower is which.
This park opened in 1901. Some of the mechanical automata in its museum are older than your grandparents' grandparents.

laia.name: Laia
laia.intro: I'm Laia and I'm SIX and three-quarters and I've been on the Ferris wheel two times!
lines: Did you know the Ferris wheel goes round and round and you can see the SEA from the top? That's true.
If you get lost you should look at the map. Press M! My mama taught me.
The church up there has a big statue of Jesus on top with his arms open. Mama says he's hugging the whole city.

rosalia.name: Rosalia
lines: Tibidabo is 512 metres high. On a very clear day you can see Montserrat's jagged outline far inland.
Be kind to anyone who has lost something. You'd be amazed what people give in thanks.
The Temple del Sagrat Cor took sixty years to build, from 1902 to 1961.

blanca.name: Blanca
lines: The Carretera de les Aigües is a flat path along the side of Collserola, with the whole city below you. Perfect for a long walk.
Sit on this terrace at dusk. The city lights come on block by block, as if someone were switching them on just for you.
Collserola is one of the largest metropolitan parks in the world — around eight thousand hectares of forest on the city's doorstep.

sergi.name: Sergi
lines: The coast road south is the old way to València, about three hundred and fifty kilometres. A lovely drive. Some other time.
This bridge is closed, I'm afraid. There's plenty to do in Barcelona in the meantime — the city is that way.
This river is the Llobregat. It rises in the Pyrenees and meets the sea just south of the city.

bruno.name: Bruno
lines: Cava is Catalonia's sparkling wine, made mostly around Sant Sadurní d'Anoia. There are several bottles of it in the kitchen already.
The birthday girl's by the window. She's asked whether you were coming about eleven times.
Alessandra's lived here a year and already knows every neighbour on the Passeig by name. And their dogs' names.

clara.name: Clara
lines: At Catalan birthdays people sometimes tug the birthday person's ears, once for every year. Gently. Mostly.
Have you tried neules? The torró shops sell them — crisp little rolled wafers, lethal with cava.
These old Eixample flats have such high ceilings — so the summer heat can rise away from you.

iker.name: Iker
lines: In Barcelona a party starts at ten and the good music starts at one. We're still in the warm-up.
If you haven't met Maria yet — she lives just north of UPF. Very organised. Terrifyingly organised.
Look at these floor tiles — hydraulic tiles. Every old flat in the Eixample has its own pattern.

lucia.name: Lucía
lines: The sardana is danced in a circle, hands joined and raised. Anyone can join — as long as they respect the count.
The Pfand desk saved my birthday budget once. Bottles, Sandra. Bottles.
Alessandra's balcony looks straight down the Passeig de Gràcia. At night the lamps look like a necklace.

PFAND_TIP: Short of money? Here's a secret: those empty bottles on the beach are worth a euro each at the Pfand desk in Carrefour Express, on the Gran Via. Deposit bottles — very German, very useful.

obj.go: Find your flat on Flor del Iliri (just east of La Rambla)

log.start: I woke up on the beach at Barceloneta — I must have dozed off watching the sunrise. Time to find my way home to Flor del Iliri, 4.
log.done: Home at last: Flor del Iliri, 4. Rosa was waiting with coffee and a raised eyebrow.

gift.name: The birthday gift

obj.buy: Buy torró for Alessandra's birthday (€12 — Casa Joan or Torrons del Mar)
obj.party: Take the torró to Alessandra's party on Passeig de Gràcia

gift.card: Sandra!! It's my BIRTHDAY PARTY tonight at my flat — Passeig de Gràcia, 47. Bring nothing but yourself (and maybe something sweet...). Can't wait! — Alessandra ✶
gift.think: Torró! Alessandra loves torró. The torró shops sell it for €12... and Sandra's purse holds exactly nothing. Hmm.

log.start: Alessandra's birthday party is tonight at her flat on Passeig de Gràcia. I want to bring her torró (€12) — but I have €0.
log.bought: Bought the torró — now, the party!
log.done: Gave Alessandra her torró at the party. She hugged me so hard I dropped a neula. Best night since I arrived.

gift.noMoney: For a birthday? Que bonic. It's €12 a bar, though, reina, and your purse sounds very quiet. Come back with twelve euros and it's yours.
gift.arrive: SANDRA! You came! Come in, come in — everyone's here! (Sandra hides her empty hands behind her back. The torró... she still needs to buy it.)
give: SANDRA! You came! And is that... torró? For me? You remembered!

(Alessandra tears off the paper, breaks off a corner, and closes her eyes.) You know what, Sandra? A year ago I didn't know a single person in this city. Now look at this room. Look at you. Thank you — truly. For coming, for the torró, for being you.
Now go and dance before Iker steals the playlist!

dog.name: The lost dog
dog.offer: My Trufa — a scruffy little thing, brown and white, red collar — slipped her lead chasing a squirrel and ran off east, all the way into the forest. My knees won't carry me up there any more. Would you look for her?
dog.accept: Oh, gràcies, gràcies! She answers to 'Trufa' and to the rustle of a biscuit packet. The forest is east, past Carrer de Nàpols.
dog.decline: I understand. If you change your mind, I'll be right here. I'm always here.
dog.remind: Any sign of Trufa? The forest is east, past Nàpols. Brown and white, red collar, terrible manners.

obj.find: Find Trufa in the eastern forest
obj.back: Bring Trufa back to Montse on La Rambla

done: TRUFA! Oh, you bad, wonderful dog! (Trufa leaps into Montse's arms and licks her chin.)
Sandra, I can't thank you enough. Here — five euros, and don't you dare argue.

And these are yours too, I think. This morning, before she ran off, Trufa fetched these chewed pages out of the park and presented them to me like a trophy. 'The Rambla Guide to Economics, Chapter 3'. You're the student — they must be meant for you.

log.start: Montse on La Rambla has lost her little dog Trufa in the eastern forest. Find her and bring her home.
log.found: Found Trufa in the forest! She's trotting at my heels. Back to Montse on La Rambla.
log.done: Trufa is home! Montse gave me €5 — and the chewed pages Trufa had proudly fetched out of the park that morning: Study Notes 3.

bike.name: The bicycle
bike.offer: I'm restoring an old roadster — lovely frame, 1970s, only needs a chain. Genís the courier has one for me at the Tibidabo funicular station, but he's stuck on his route up there. Could you collect it? Bring me the chain and the bike is yours. I have far too many.
bike.accept: Fantàstic! The funicular station is north, past the Diagonal, at the foot of the mountain path. Genís has a cargo bike and a very loud whistle.
bike.decline: No pressure. The bike isn't going anywhere — that's rather the problem.
bike.remind: The chain's with Genís at the funicular station, north of the Diagonal.
bike.handoff: Ah, Jordi's chain! Here, wrapped in its paper. Tell him he owes me a coffee. He always owes me a coffee.

obj.fetch: Collect the chain from Genís at the Tibidabo funicular station
obj.back: Take the chain to Jordi on Carrer d'Aragó

done: That's the one! Give me two minutes... (clink, clack, whirr) ...there.
She's yours: an old bicycle, ridden far more often than she's been washed. Press B to hop on. Three times faster than walking — but not indoors, and not on the sand!

log.start: Jordi, the bike mechanic on Carrer d'Aragó, needs a chain from Genís the courier at the Tibidabo funicular station.
log.got: Collected the chain from Genís. Back to Jordi on Carrer d'Aragó.
log.done: Jordi fitted the chain and gave me an OLD BICYCLE! Press B to ride.

crema.name: The stonemason's sweet tooth
crema.offer: Can I tell you a secret? I've had a craving all week. A crema catalana — a proper one, from Cafè de la Rambla, where they torch the sugar to order. I can't leave the scaffold. Bring me one and I'll make it worth your while.
crema.accept: You're a saint. Well — not an official one. Cafè de la Rambla, just west of the Rambla on València. €15, and worth every cèntim.
crema.decline: Ah well. The craving will keep. It's been keeping all week.
crema.remind: Cafè de la Rambla — the crema catalana. I can almost hear the caramel crack.

obj.buy: Buy a crema catalana at Cafè de la Rambla (€15)
obj.back: Deliver the crema catalana to Pau at the Sagrada Família

done: (Pau cracks the caramel with the handle of a chisel and closes his eyes.) Perfecte.
Here's €20 for your trouble. And a thing worth knowing: this basilica has never had a state budget. Every stone is paid for by donations and visitors' tickets — including, in a small way, yours.

log.start: Pau, a stonemason at the Sagrada Família, is craving a crema catalana from Cafè de la Rambla (€15).
log.done: Delivered the crema catalana. Pau paid me €20 and told me the basilica is built entirely from donations and tickets.

brush.name: The missing brush
brush.offer: I've lost my best sable brush — the tiny one, with C.F. scratched on the handle. I was sketching the Cascada in the Ciutadella yesterday and it must have rolled into the grass. I can't restore a halo with a broom. Would you look for it?
brush.accept: Thank you! The Cascada is at the north end of the Parc de la Ciutadella, in the east of the city.
brush.decline: Of course. I'll keep squinting with the second-best brush.
brush.remind: Any luck with my brush? It'll be somewhere in the grass near the Cascada, in the Ciutadella.

obj.find: Find Carme's sable brush near the Cascada in the Ciutadella
obj.back: Return the brush to Carme at the MNAC

done: My brush! Oh, you lovely person. Halos everywhere are safe again.
Here — a cafè amb llet and a croissant from the museum café. I bought them for myself, but you've earned them more.
brush.doneFull: Your bag is full, so take a few euros for the museum café instead. You've earned it.

log.start: Carme, a restorer at the MNAC, lost her sable brush near the Cascada in the Parc de la Ciutadella.
log.got: Found Carme's brush in the grass by the Cascada. Back to the MNAC.
log.done: Returned Carme's brush. She gave me a cafè amb llet and a croissant from the museum café.

balloon.name: The balloon at Tibidabo
balloon.offer: My balloon flew away! It's red and it got stuck by the Ferris wheel and now it's too high and Mama says it's gone forever. Can you get it? Please? PLEASE?
balloon.accept: YES! It's by the big wheel. Over there! THERE!
balloon.remind: It's by the Ferris wheel! It's RED! Did you see it?

obj.find: Rescue Laia's balloon by the Ferris wheel
obj.back: Give the balloon back to Laia

done: MY BALLOON! (She hugs it so hard it squeaks.) Mama! Mama! She got it!
Rosalia: Moltes gràcies. Here — a chocolate bar and an orange juice. It's all I've got in my bag, but it's yours.
balloon.doneFull: Rosalia: Your bag looks full to bursting — here, take a few coins instead.

log.start: Laia lost her red balloon by the Ferris wheel at Tibidabo. Rescue it!
log.got: Untangled Laia's balloon from the railing by the Ferris wheel.
log.done: Rescued Laia's balloon! Her mother Rosalia gave me a chocolate bar and an orange juice.

profbook.name: The professor's book
profbook.offer: Sandra, a small favour. I lent my Principles of Economics to Alice, who is, I gather, home sick on Carrer de Balmes. I need it for Monday's lecture and would rather not deliver it from memory. Could you collect it for me?
profbook.accept: Excellent. Carrer de Balmes is the westernmost street of the grid. Do wish Alice a swift recovery from me.
profbook.decline: No matter. I'll improvise. Economists are excellent at improvising; we call it 'modelling'.
profbook.remind: The textbook, Sandra? Alice has it — Carrer de Balmes.
profbook.handoff: Oriol's book! Yes, take it — I'm far too feverish for elasticity. I've put a get-well card in it as a bookmark. Tell him it's a thank-you.

obj.fetch: Collect Prof. Oriol's textbook from Alice on Carrer de Balmes
obj.back: Return the textbook to Prof. Oriol at UPF

done: My book! And annotated with... a get-well card. Charming.
Here, €5 for your trouble. And a joke, free of charge: an economist is someone who sees something working in practice and wonders whether it would work in theory.

log.start: Prof. Oriol lent his textbook to Alice, home sick on Carrer de Balmes. Collect it and return it to him at UPF.
log.got: Alice handed over the professor's textbook, with a get-well card inside. Back to UPF.
log.done: Returned Prof. Oriol's textbook. €5 and an economics joke.

flour.name: Flour for the baker
flour.offer: Disaster! I'm out of rye flour. No rye, no Vollkornbrot, and without Vollkornbrot my German regulars look at me like orphans. Carrefour on the Gran Via stocks it — €10 a sack. Would you fetch one?
flour.accept: Merci — sorry, danke — sorry, GRÀCIES. Carrefour Express, down on the Gran Via by the sea.
flour.decline: I'll try to survive on wheat. It's going to be a long week.
flour.remind: Rye flour, from Carrefour on the Gran Via. My starter is getting anxious.

obj.buy: Buy rye flour at Carrefour Express on the Gran Via (€10)
obj.back: Deliver the rye flour to Ferran at Cafè Berlín

done: Rye! Beautiful, beautiful rye!
Here's €14 — and a Vollkornbrot, fresh from the oven, on the house. Guten Appetit!
flour.doneFull: Your bag's full, so I'll give you the bread's worth in coins instead.

log.start: Ferran at Cafè Berlín is out of rye flour. Buy a sack at Carrefour Express (€10) and deliver it.
log.done: Delivered the rye flour. Ferran paid €14 and gave me a free Vollkornbrot.

rivalry.name: The torró rivalry
rivalry.offer: Between us: everyone's talking about Neus's soft torró down at Torrons del Mar. Softer than mine, they say. I must know. But I can't walk in there — she'd see me coming a kilometre off. Buy me a bar? €12. I'll make it very much worth your while.
rivalry.accept: Discreetly, eh? Torrons del Mar, down south near the beach on the Gran Via. Tell no one.
rivalry.decline: Forget I asked. I never asked. What torró?
rivalry.remind: Any... parcel for me? From the seaside establishment?
rivalry.ownTorro: This is MY torró, noia. I know my own almonds. I need HERS — Torrons del Mar, by the beach.

obj.buy: Buy a bar of torró at Torrons del Mar (€12)
obj.back: Bring the rival torró to Joan at Casa Joan

done: (Joan unwraps it, sniffs it, tastes it, and is silent for a long moment.) ...It's good. It's very good. Don't tell her I said so.
Here — €18, and a bar of my own on the house, so you can be the judge.
rivalry.doneFull: Your bag's full — I'll add the price of my bar to the coins instead.

log.start: Joan of Torrons Casa Joan secretly wants to taste his rival's torró. Buy a bar at Torrons del Mar (€12) and bring it to him.
log.done: Brought Joan his rival's torró. €18 and a free bar of his own. The rivalry continues, deliciously.

hat.name: The fisherman's hat
hat.offer: Avi Tomàs lost his cap in the wind yesterday — it blew right up the beach and got stuck at the edge of the eastern forest. He won't admit it, but he's miserable without it. Could you fetch it back? He'll thank you, I promise.
hat.accept: Gràcies! It's navy blue with a brass anchor. The forest edge is east, where the beach ends.
hat.decline: No worries. He'll just keep touching his head and sighing.
hat.remind: The cap's at the eastern forest edge. Navy, with a brass anchor. He keeps touching his head.
hat.giveHint: You found it! Give it to Avi — he's right there, pretending not to care.

obj.find: Find Tomàs's cap at the eastern forest edge
obj.back: Return the cap to Tomàs on the beach

done: My cap! Where — the forest? That wind! (He puts it on and is instantly ten years younger.)
Here — five euros, and three good shells I picked up this morning.
And these pages blew into my fishing spot yesterday — the same wind that took my cap. 'Chapter 5: Comparative Advantage', fish and loaves. You're a student; you have them.

log.start: Núria's grandfather Tomàs lost his cap to the wind; it's stuck at the eastern forest edge. Retrieve it and return it to him on the beach.
log.got: Found Tomàs's cap caught in a bush at the forest edge.
log.done: Returned Tomàs's cap. €5, three seashells — and Study Notes 5, blown into his fishing spot by the same wind.

camera.name: The tourist's camera
camera.offer: I've had the worst morning. I visited Casa Vicens and left my good camera in a cupboard — I put it down to take off my jacket and just walked out. Could you fetch it for me? I'll make it worth your while, I swear.
camera.accept: You're a star! Casa Vicens is in the north-west of the grid, facing Carrer de Provença. The cupboard inside!
camera.decline: Okay... I'll keep taking photos with my eyes.
camera.remind: My camera — in the cupboard at Casa Vicens, north-west, on Provença.

obj.fetch: Fetch Marta's camera from the cupboard in Casa Vicens
obj.back: Return the camera to Marta outside Casa Batlló

done: MY CAMERA! (She checks it all over.) Not a scratch!
Here — €10, and take my old spare camera too. I never use it any more. With the camera on you, you can take a picture anytime — just pick it out of your backpack.

log.start: Marta, a photographer outside Casa Batlló, left her camera in a cupboard at Casa Vicens. Return it to her.
log.got: Found Marta's camera in the cupboard at Casa Vicens.
log.done: Returned Marta's camera. €10 and her old spare camera: with it on me, I can take a photo anytime from my backpack.

grail.name: The bookseller's grail
grail.offer: 'The Bookseller's Ghost', by Elvira Quintana i Font, the green cloth edition. I have heard that a copy is in the hands of a student who lives by the Ciutadella — a young woman who, they say, trades in flowers, not euros. If you could persuade her, I would give you something rare in return.
grail.accept: Bless you. By the Ciutadella, on València. Flowers, remember — not euros.
grail.decline: Twenty-nine years. I can wait a little longer.
grail.remind: Any word of the Ghost? The student by the Ciutadella. She trades in flowers.
grail.albaAsk: 'The Bookseller's Ghost'? Mm, I have it — it's right there on my table. I don't need the book, but what I do need are some flowers to fill this empty vase. Bring me five wildflowers and it's yours.
albaGive: Five wildflowers! (She arranges them in the vase one at a time, humming.) There. Perfect.
And here's the book. Tell the bookseller it's been read with love.

obj.find: Find the student by the Ciutadella who has 'The Bookseller's Ghost'
obj.back: Take 'The Bookseller's Ghost' to Ponç at Llibreria El Drac

done: (Ponç holds the book very still, as if it might fly away.) Twenty-nine years.

Thank you. I have nothing as rare to give you... except this: pages I found pressed inside a second-hand paperback from a job lot last month. 'The Rambla Guide to Economics, Chapter 4'. Some student's treasure. Now yours.

log.start: Ponç at Llibreria El Drac has hunted for 'The Bookseller's Ghost' for years. A student by the Ciutadella has a copy — and trades in flowers.
log.ask: Alba has the book! She'll trade it for five wildflowers to fill her empty vase.
log.got: Alba traded me 'The Bookseller's Ghost' for five wildflowers. The vase looks lovely. Back to Ponç.
log.done: Brought Ponç 'The Bookseller's Ghost'. In return: Study Notes 4, found pressed inside a second-hand paperback.

obj.sit: Sit the economics exam with Prof. Oriol at UPF

log.start: Prof. Oriol says it is time for my final assessment. Five questions, one from each chapter of the Rambla Guide.
log.done: I PASSED! Prof. Oriol presented me with the Universitat Pompeu Fabra Diploma of Economics. Semester complete — Barcelona is mine.

NOTE_GIVE.rosa: Oh! Before I forget — I found these pages at the back of the cupboard when you moved in. The last Erasmus student who had your room left them: 'The Rambla Guide to Economics, Chapter 1'. They say there are five chapters floating around Barcelona, and anyone who has all five sails through the UPF economics exam. Probably a legend. Probably.
NOTE_GIVE.maria: Here — take my copy of Chapter 2 of the Rambla Guide. I have it memorised, and I made a laminated backup anyway. Find all five chapters and you'll be ready for Oriol's exam.

ORIOL_STATES.wait: The exam is still being prepared. Meanwhile, I hear there are many people in Barcelona who could use a helping hand.
ORIOL_STATES.study: You have seen enough of Barcelona. You should be studying for the exam.
ORIOL_STATES.ready: It is time for your final assessment. I hope you are prepared for the exam.
ORIOL_STATES.pass: Congratulations, Sandra. Five out of five would have been showing off; four is splendid. The Universitat Pompeu Fabra Diploma of Economics is yours.
ORIOL_STATES.pass5: Full marks. I have been setting this exam for nineteen years and I find I have nothing to add. The Universitat Pompeu Fabra Diploma of Economics is yours, Sandra.
ORIOL_STATES.fail: Hmm. We shall call that a mock exam and never speak of it again. Come back whenever you're ready to try once more.
ORIOL_STATES.after: A graduate of the Rambla Guide! Go and enjoy your city, Sandra. Barcelona is a far better teacher than I am.

PHONE.intro: Sandra picks up the heavy old telephone. It still has a dial.
PHONE.hello: Mama: Sandra! Schatz! Are you eating properly? Are you wearing sun cream? Tell me everything.
PHONE.bye: Mama: Bis bald, Schatz. Papa says hello and asks if you've found good bread yet. We love you. Call on Sunday!

INTRO_TEXT: Bon dia, Sandra! You wake to the hush of small waves. The sun is up over Barceloneta — you must have dozed off on the sand after watching the sunrise.
You're a German economics student on Erasmus at Universitat Pompeu Fabra, and home is a little flat at Flor del Iliri, 4, which you share with Rosa. Your purse holds exactly €0.
Walk with the ARROW KEYS or WASD. Press SPACE or ENTER to talk, read, pick things up and open doors. I opens your backpack, M the map, J your journal. In choices, ENTER confirms and SPACE backs out.
TOUCH: Walk with the pad. Tap A to talk, read, pick things up and open doors, and B to go back. BAG, MAP and LOG open your backpack, the map and your journal; ☰ is the menu.
La Rambla runs straight up from this beach into the city. Your street, Flor del Iliri, is just east of it. Benvinguda a Barcelona!

objs.t: Sandra's bed, by the window side. The pillow still has a faint dent shaped like a long night of studying.
A watercolour of the Barceloneta beach at dawn. Rosa painted it. It is honestly quite good.
Rosa's bed, on the far side of the room, made with military precision. There is a small stuffed dragon on the pillow.
Sandra's desk.
phone
A little round table with two mismatched mugs. One says 'Tarragona', the other 'Giessen an der Lahn'.
The kitchen corner: a two-ring hob, a coffee pot, and a jar of sugar Rosa guards like a dragon.
The fridge. Rosa's yoghurts are labelled ROSA. Sandra's side contains one lemon, optimistically.
A poster for a flamenco night in Gràcia, signed by the dancers. Alessandra went twice.
Alessandra's bed, heaped with cushions and at least one coat belonging to a guest.
The table, crowded with crisps, olives, a tortilla and a very large bowl of something pink.
Alice's bed: a nest of blankets, tissues, and a thermometer she keeps checking in hope.
A table of get-well cards, cough drops and a half-finished jigsaw of the Sagrada Família (the towers are the hard part).
Frames of pressed flowers, each labelled in Latin in tiny handwriting.
Alba's bed, with a quilt embroidered with ferns.
Maria's desk: three highlighters, a ruler, and a laminated timetable colour-coded to the quarter-hour.
Maria's bed, corners folded like an envelope. A small red-and-yellow flag hangs above it.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
A gleaming brass espresso machine, older than Empar and treated with more respect.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
The chalkboard: CAFÈ 1,50 · CROISSANT 1,50 · SUC DE TARONJA 2,00 · CREMA CATALANA 15,00 — 'la millor de Barcelona, cremada al moment'.
Loaves ranked by darkness, from pale Weissbrot to a Vollkornbrot so dense it could anchor a boat.
The bread oven, radiating a heat that smells exactly like a Saturday morning in Giessen.
Loaves ranked by darkness, from pale Weissbrot to a Vollkornbrot so dense it could anchor a boat.
Boxes of nougat stacked in careful towers: hard, soft, chocolate, and one labelled simply 'SECRET'.
Boxes of nougat stacked in careful towers: hard, soft, chocolate, and one labelled simply 'SECRET'.
A photograph of Joan's grandfather in 1931, standing proudly beside a cart of almonds.
Boxes of nougat stacked in careful towers, each tied with blue-and-white ribbon like a tiny sailor.
Boxes of nougat stacked in careful towers, each tied with blue-and-white ribbon like a tiny sailor.
A painting of a fishing boat called 'Neus II'. Nobody has ever seen a 'Neus I'.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
Chilled cabinets humming contentedly: milk, cheese, yoghurts, and forty kinds of olive.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
Well-stocked shelves, neatly faced and labelled — the sign of a shop that knows its regulars.
Books shelved by whim: poetry beside plumbing, a cookbook wedged between two popes. Ponç insists there is a system.
Books shelved by whim: poetry beside plumbing, a cookbook wedged between two popes. Ponç insists there is a system.
A shelf of second-hand paperbacks, soft as cloth. Several have other people's bus tickets inside.
A shelf of second-hand paperbacks, soft as cloth. Several have other people's bus tickets inside.
A reading armchair, sagging in exactly the shape of a person who has been reading for thirty years.
A painted dragon curled around the words 'El Drac'. It looks well-read.
The blackboard: a supply-and-demand diagram, half erased, and the words 'NO EXAM TALK BEFORE COFFEE'.
Working papers in teetering stacks, and a small tarnished trophy: 'Faculty Football Cup — Runners-up, 2011'.
The noticeboard: seminar times, a lost cat called Keynes, and 'Erasmus welcome paella — Friday!'

UNIVERSITY LIBRARY — UPSTAIRS ▲
Biblioteca de la UPF, 1st floor. Reading room open to all. Silence, please.

1st FLOOR — BIBLIOTECA UPF
▼ Down to the Department of Economics.
NO BOOK LEAVES THIS FLOOR.
The eastern windows: blues and greens, the colours of dawn and the Nativity. The light falls across the floor like water.
The western windows: reds, oranges and golds, the colours of sunset and the Passion. The stone glows as if warm to the touch.
The altar beneath a hanging canopy of lamps and grapevines. Above it, the vaulting opens like a forest canopy.
A plaster model of a tower, made with Gaudí's own hanging-chain method. Workers still consult models like this one.
Scaffolding, dust sheets and a thermos. A sign reads: OBRES — WORK IN PROGRESS (since 1882).
The apse of Sant Climent de Taüll, painted around 1123: Christ in Majesty, eyes wide, holding a book that says 'Ego sum lux mundi' — I am the light of the world.
A Romanesque fresco of saints in a row, their robes the colour of rust and ripe apricots, their expressions politely astonished.
A painted Last Supper from a Pyrenean church, the table laid with fish and very small loaves.
A carved wooden Virgin and Child from the twelfth century, the paint worn gold at the edges.
An enamelled reliquary casket from Limoges, glowing blue and gold.
Carme's restoration table: a magnifying lamp, cotton buds, tiny jars of pigment and a very empty brush-shaped space.
A stone capital carved with lions eating, very politely, a smaller lion.
A Gothic angel with one wing missing and an expression of great patience.
The great window over the Passeig de Gràcia, framed in bone-like columns. The glass ripples like water.
Stained glass in sea-greens and blues. From inside, the whole city looks as if it's underwater.
The mushroom-shaped fireplace nook, with benches either side for courting couples and a chaperone.
A model of the scaly roof, with the four-armed cross on its turret — Sant Jordi's lance in the dragon's back.
Two hundred and seventy catenary brick arches run the length of the attic, like the ribs of a whale.
A hanging-chain model: little bags of shot on strings, making the shape of arches upside down.
A model of the roof, with its helmeted warrior chimneys standing guard.
The smoking room's ceiling glimmers with honeycomb plaster and painted palm leaves.
A little tiled fountain. Once, a waterfall ran through the garden outside.

TIBIDABO_PLAQUE: PARC D'ATRACCIONS DEL TIBIDABO. Opened in 1901 on the highest summit of Collserola, 512 metres up. The name comes from the Latin 'tibi dabo' — 'I will give you'. The Avió, a replica aeroplane from 1928, still circles over the city. Beside the park rises the Temple del Sagrat Cor, finished in 1961.
